📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Juggling between three languages on a daily basis, Iris is known for her love of linguistics, arts, web design and typography, as well as her goldmine of … More about Iris ↬.

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

AI is changing how we design and build, and it isn’t slowing down. On December 1, 2026, SmashingConf is hosting the AI 2027 Conference, a live online half day event to take stock of where AI stands today, what we can expect in 2027, and where teams are getting it right.

It has been revealed that with AI maturing, it’s clear we need to learn how AI can elevate your workflow as a UX designer and Design System engineer. Most of us are still figuring it out and trying to work smarter in this latest world, so we invited industry experts who have been doing this for a while. They show their experience and tell you what works and what doesn’t, so you don’t have to figure it all out yourself.

Every session is practical. Speakers show how they actually work: their tools, their setups, and the small things that are easy to miss. The event ends with moderated breakout rooms, where you can bring your own workflow questions. See you there?

Industry observers note that this conference is dedicated to designers and engineers (front-end, UI, UX) who want to understand how AI can improve the way their team works, without the hype. If you’re interested in AI-ready design systems, AI and Figma, harness engineering, agentic AI UX patterns, and AI workflows for design and engineering teams, this conference is right up your alley!

Showing, not telling: All sessions will be highly practical, focusing on how to integrate AI in your daily work and what to expect in 2027.

According to recent reports, for our AI 2027 Conference, your friendly host Vitaly will welcome you and swiftly explain how the event will run. We can’t wait to meet you!

Recent findings suggest that AI is moving fast. With it come new workflows in product teams, new design patterns, new user expectations and new ways of thinking about building and designing for AI.Let’s look at where things stand today. A lot changed in 2026, and there are things we can now design and build that simply weren’t possible a year ago. We’ll cover the patterns taking shape heading into 2027, from multi-modal experiences to accessibility, and what tends to go wrong along the way. A massive part of that is designing for trust, so people feel confident using what we make.What makes AI products reliable in practice? We’ll look at how teams cut down on hallucinations with better context, a well-built harness and sensible guardrails. Then we’ll finish with what’s coming in 2027, including new experiments, regulations and a few takeaways to bring back to your team.Roll up your sleeves for a packed session, full of real-life examples and design patterns.

Great AI-powered products live at the intersection of engineering depth, design craft and product thinking. In this talk, Anna Arteeva demonstrates how to build real, working AI experiences, not just one-shot prototypes that fall apart the moment someone uses them.You’ll learn how to design and prototype an AI-powered experience from scratch, with functionality built on LLMs, voice and image generation logic. Anna will also show how to add that little bit of delight to your app, and how it can respond to different types of input, whatever the person on the other side of the screen gives you: text, voice or images.

What coding agents need from your design system docs, and how to write it.Documentation is the part of the design system teams are least happy with, and it’s been that way for years. Luke Murphy looks at how we ended up with docs nobody reads and why agents change the picture. Then, drawing on DS ARC’s tests of real design systems, he walks through the small writing changes that make docs work for agents and people alike.This is a talk from our friends at zeroheight. Thank you for joining in!

Industry observers note that the massive question for many teams is how to get your code and your Figma file talking to each other. In this session, Christine Vallaure shares how she has set this up in practice: going from code to Figma instead of the other way around, moving back and forth between the two for the best result, and what that means for how we work.You’ll hear why design system basics suddenly matter a lot more, why naming things well pays off, and why AI builders so often produce code that looks like your design system but still has to be rebuilt. She’ll also explain the engineering side that designers don’t always see, like the checks and files your developers set up, so you know how it works and what to ask for. Along the way, she covers the problems you’re likely to run into, what to keep in mind, and where Storybook fits in.Expect plenty of small tips and tricks you can take straight back to your team.

AI flipped the script on the traditional, linear design system workflow. That’s okay. We’re all experimenting, and nobody has this figured out yet.TJ Pitre has spent the past two years working with dozens of teams to find the flow that fits them. He’ll show three alternative workflows live. Which one fits depends on you: how big your design system is, how big your team is, how much effort you’re willing to put in, and how well it needs to scale.The goal is to get you thinking, and to send you back to your team with a few workflows worth trying.

Sources indicate that brad Frost shares his actual workflow for building products with AI and a design system. He’ll show the setup, architecture, and tools he uses to keep AI on the rails of his components, tokens, and patterns.Expect live building, real design decisions, and plenty of practical tricks along the way. You’ll see how it all works together and leave with ideas to apply to your own design system and workflow.

Designing & Building AI Experiences in 2027The way we design and build is changing massively, and we are all adapting to the new reality. In this session, we’ll talk about how to design and build AI experiences that actually work, and are a delight to use. Bring your questions, post your problems and work with Vitaly and Anna, and all the other attendees, to solve them together. A will (technically a "last will and testament") is a legal document that specifies how your assets should be distributed after your death. It must go through probate — a court-supervised process that validates the will, pays debts and taxes, and distributes assets to beneficiaries. A living trust (specifically a revocable living trust) is a legal entity you create during your lifetime that holds your assets. When you die, the successor trustee distributes those assets according to the trust terms — without court involvement.

According to recent reports, the critical distinction is probate. In states with expensive or slow probate processes — California, Latest York, Florida, and many others — a living trust pays for itself many times over. In states with simplified probate procedures (like Texas or Wisconsin for small estates), the cost advantage of a trust is smaller but the privacy and incapacity benefits still apply.

Industry observers note that you need both: A trust does not name guardians for minor children (only a will can do that), and a trust only controls assets that have been formally transferred into it. A pour-over will acts as a safety net — it directs any assets not in the trust at your death to pour into the trust, where they are distributed according to the trust terms. The pour-over will still goes through probate, but it ensures nothing falls through the cracks.

The term "living trust" almost always refers to a revocable living trust — one you can change, amend, or dissolve at any time during your lifetime. You remain the trustee, manage the assets as you always have, and pay taxes on trust income using your personal Social Security number. For income tax purposes, a revocable trust is invisible — the IRS treats it as if it does not exist.

An irrevocable trust is fundamentally different. Once established, you cannot easily modify it, and the assets inside it are no longer legally yours. This permanence provides two powerful advantages:.

The federal estate tax exemption is $13.61 million per person ($27.22 million for married couples) in 2026, but this historically high exemption is scheduled to sunset after 2025, potentially dropping to approximately $7 million per person. FIRE households who have built $3 million to $10 million in net worth through decades of saving and investment growth should monitor this sunset closely. If the exemption drops, irrevocable trusts become relevant at much lower wealth levels.

In a recent development, for most FIRE households with $1 million to $5 million in net worth, a revocable living trust provides the right balance of control, flexibility, and probate avoidance. Irrevocable structures become compelling only when estate tax exposure is real or asset protection needs are elevated.

Estate planning is governed primarily by state law, and the value of a living trust versus a will varies significantly depending on where you live.

Nine states are community property states: Arizona, California, Idaho, Louisiana, Nevada, Latest Mexico, Texas, Washington, and Wisconsin. In these states, most assets acquired during marriage are owned 50/50 by both spouses regardless of whose name is on the title. At death, only the deceased spouse's half passes through their estate initiative.

The remaining 41 states follow common law (also called "equitable distribution"). Ownership depends on whose name is on the title. This distinction affects how assets pass at death and whether a trust or will provides better spousal protection.

Use this framework to determine whether you need a trust, a will, or both:.

Remember that a trust only controls assets titled in the trust's name. After creating a trust, you must fund it by re-titling your bank accounts, brokerage accounts, and real estate into the trust. Unfunded trusts — trusts that exist on paper but hold no assets — provide zero benefit. The pour-over will catches stragglers, but relying entirely on the pour-over defeats the purpose because those assets still go through probate.

The most common estate planning mistake with trusts is failing to fund them. Creating a trust document costs $1,500 to $5,000, but if you never transfer your bank accounts, brokerage accounts, and real estate into the trust, it provides zero probate avoidance. After signing your trust, immediately re-title assets into the trust name. Your attorney should provide a funding checklist. An unfunded trust sitting in a drawer is an expensive piece of paper — not an estate strategy.

Yes. A pour-over will catches any assets not transferred into your trust during your lifetime and directs them into the trust at death. A will is also the only legal document that can name guardians for minor children. Every trust-based estate blueprint should include a pour-over will.

Industry observers note that A revocable living trust prepared by an estate planning attorney typically costs $1,500 to $5,000, depending on complexity and your location. This usually includes the trust document, pour-over will, powers of attorney, healthcare directives, and initial funding guidance. Online trust services cost $200 to $500 but may not address state-specific issues or complex situations.

Yes, and you should be. With a revocable living trust, you serve as both the grantor (creator) and the trustee (manager). You maintain full control over all trust assets during your lifetime. You name a successor trustee who takes over only if you become incapacitated or die.

It has been revealed that A revocable living trust does not reduce estate taxes — the IRS treats it as if it does not exist for income and estate tax purposes. However, a trust can be structured with provisions (such as an A/B trust or disclaimer trust) that maximize the use of both spouses' estate tax exemptions. For estate tax reduction, irrevocable trusts are the primary tool.

A revocable trust can be changed, amended, or dissolved at any time. You maintain full control. An irrevocable trust generally cannot be changed after creation, and the assets inside it are no longer legally yours. Revocable trusts provide probate avoidance and incapacity planning. Irrevocable trusts provide estate tax reduction and asset protection.

Industry observers note that without a trust, each state where you own real property requires a separate probate proceeding (called ancillary probate), multiplying costs and complexity. Transferring out-of-state property into a living trust eliminates ancillary probate entirely — the successor trustee can transfer or sell the property without court involvement in any state.

The living trust vs will decision is not about which is better — it is about which is better for your specific situation. For estates with more than $100,000 in probatable assets, especially in high-cost probate states, a revocable living trust saves thousands of dollars and months of delay while providing incapacity protection and privacy that a will cannot match. For smaller estates in simplified-probate states, a well-drafted will with proper beneficiary designations may be all you need. Either way, the worst estate plan is no estate plan. More than 60% of American adults have neither a will nor a trust, leaving their families to navigate probate without guidance, pay avoidable costs, and endure unnecessary delays during the most difficult time of their lives.

Nan Goldin to debut newly introduced film exploring nature and extinction in first UK solo museum show in over two decades

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (516 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theartnewspaper

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • For audiences who associate the US photographer Nan Goldin with the friends and lovers of her slideshow The Ballad of Sexual Dependency (1973-86), her forthcoming Hayward Gallery exhibition may come as a surprise.
  • What links these subjects to the photographs that established her reputation?
  • Nan Goldin, Still from You never did anything wrong, Part II, 2026.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For audiences who associate the US photographer Nan Goldin with the friends and lovers of her slideshow The Ballad of Sexual Dependency (1973-86), her forthcoming Hayward Gallery exhibition may come as a surprise. Animals, a solar eclipse and footage salvaged from nature documentaries will feature in Goldin’s first institutional solo show in the UK since her 2002 retrospective at the Whitechapel Gallery.

What links these subjects to the photographs that established her reputation? According to the Hayward’s chief curator, Rachel Thomas, the connection lies in the relationships Goldin creates through the camera, rather than the identities of those who appear before it. In Thomas’s reading, Goldin’s focus on queer communities and chosen family has widened to embrace the natural world.

Nan Goldin, Still from You never did anything wrong, Part II, 2026.

© Nan Goldin, courtesy the artist and Gagosian.

Industry observers note that rather than being a retrospective, the exhibition You Never Did Anything Wrong presents new and recent work by Goldin. Thomas, who worked with the photographer at the Irish Museum of Modern Art in 2017, tells The Art Newspaper: “I wanted to collaborate again to reveal where her practice is moving now.” Four years in the making, the exhibition is the Hayward’s contribution to the Southbank Centre’s 75th-anniversary programme devoted to “visionaries who have fundamentally redefined culture”.

It has been revealed that the show’s centrepiece will be the premiere of You never did anything wrong, Part II (2026). Created with the film-maker David Sherman, it draws on 16mm nature documentaries from the 1960s and 70s, and damaged soundtracks from old films, with a new score by the British musician Mica Levi. Goldin turns material associated with explaining the natural world into an abstract meditation on animals, land and impending extinction.

Nan Goldin, Still from You never did anything wrong, Part I, 2024.

© Nan Goldin, courtesy the artist and Gagosian.

According to recent reports, it accompanies You never did anything wrong, Part I (2024), which centres on a solar eclipse and draws on a myth of animals stealing the sun. Together, the films bring Goldin’s work into a world without human protagonists.

Elsewhere, Stendhal Syndrome (2024), receiving its UK premiere, places photographs of her friends and lovers in dialogue with classical art, accompanied by a score by Soundwalk Collective. Memory Lost (2019-21), meanwhile, returns to addiction, connecting personal experience to Goldin’s campaigning with Pain (Prescription Addiction Intervention Now), the group she founded to confront the opioid crisis in the US.

Art of intimacy: Young Love (2024) is one of Goldin’s works in Stendhal Syndrome © Nan Goldin; courtesy the artist and Gagosian.

For Thomas, compassion connects these changing subjects. Goldin’s importance lies partly in her refusal to maintain a distance from the people she photographs, with the exhibition proposing that this approach can extend beyond her own community. “What endures across every medium and chapter is an exploration of compassion,” Thomas claims. “Goldin simply expands the horizon of who and what is embraced by her gaze.”.

• You Never Did Anything Wrong, Hayward Gallery, London, 24 November-14 March 2027.

A latest iPhone camera app, HyperCam Trigger, aims to make it easier for mobile photographers to nail the perfect action shot, group portrait, or lightning photo.

In a recent development, hyperCam Trigger uses various listening and detection methods to fire the iPhone’s camera at the right moment. For example, when photographing sports, children, or pets, the app can trip the shutter as soon as motion appears in the frame.

Recent findings suggest that meanwhile, for group portraits, which typically rely on a self-timer, HyperCam can listen for someone in the frame to clap, triggering an immediate shot. People can customize the sensitivity for the app and the delay between detection and shooting.

Industry observers note that the app’s original purpose, which remains a core focus, was to make it easier to photograph lightning. It can use sound for this as well, though thunder arrives well after the flash of lightning itself. The app can also trigger a shot when it detects a sudden surge of light hitting the camera.

Sources indicate that hyperCam can also trigger the shutter under other conditions, including camera shake, such as when the iPhone moves or tilts, or complete stability, such as when it is mounted on a tripod. Additionally, it can capture timelapse photos when it detects changes in light or motion, or wait to fire until someone in the frame smiles.

Lightning triggers are not a upcoming concept in photography. Photographers with DSLRs and mirrorless cameras have been using them for years, and new ones hit the market every so often, like the Bolt Hunter earlier this year.

Recent findings suggest that lightning triggers rely on the same principle as HyperCam: it is simply impossible for a photographer to manually press the shutter fast enough to catch fleeting events like lightning. Photographers can certainly try and can improve their odds by firing off long, rapid bursts of frames. However, assistance is required for consistent success.

HyperCam Trigger is available now in the App Store for free.

However, some features are locked behind a paywall, including subject filters, short event video recording with frame extraction, detection zones, longer pre-trigger buffers, longer bursts, RAW recording, HDR, and more. HyperCam Pro is available for $3.99 per month, $22.99 per year, or $44.99 for lifetime access.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Melbourne-based studio Pepper & Well took cues from crisscrossing concrete walls and ceiling beams when designing Lumeah, a fresh en-suite for a house by celebrated architect Paul Couch.
  • Located in Macedon, central Victoria, the linear single-storey house was completed in 2006 by the late Couch, who passed away earlier this year.
  • When latest owners bought the property in 2018, they felt the layout and finishes of the main bathroom didn’t meet the standards of the rest of the house.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photography by Tom Ross.

Melbourne-based studio Pepper & Well took cues from crisscrossing concrete walls and ceiling beams when designing Lumeah, a fresh en-suite for a house by celebrated architect Paul Couch.

Located in Macedon, central Victoria, the linear single-storey house was completed in 2006 by the late Couch, who passed away earlier this year.

When latest owners bought the property in 2018, they felt the layout and finishes of the main bathroom didn’t meet the standards of the rest of the house.

They asked Pepper & Well to upgrade it and make it more accessible.

“There was an opportunity to make the space more comfortable and practical as they aged,” noted lead architect Andy Dal Pozzo.

The previous layout included a WC, an enclosed shower and a step-in plunge pool, all within a space just 3.5 metres long.

Pepper & Well’s scheme removed the plunge, allowing space for a larger WC and for an open shower to be built in place of the old frosted-glass enclosure.

The defining move was the addition of a cast-concrete element that partitions the toilet and shower areas.

This incorporates an informal bench, allowing for seated showers if preferred.

The geometry of this element clearly references the house’s exposed concrete structure, a rhythmic arrangement of concrete beams over concrete walls.

“Our approach began with understanding the logic of Paul’s work,” explained Dal Pozzo.

“We wanted the renovation to share the original architecture’s material honesty and clarity, while remaining recognisable as a new contribution,” he said.

A change in floor surface marks the junction between old and new.

While most of the room features the bluestone flooring installed 20 years ago, the toilet and shower have a surface of crazy-paved slate.

The stone is the same Mintaro Brown Back slate that Couch installed in the bathroom of his own house, Toolern Vale.

“Laid in crazy paving beside the retained bluestone, it introduces a distinct texture with a direct connection to Paul’s work,” stated Dal Pozzo.

“Both materials remain clearly legible.”.

The rest of the room was left largely intact, including the solid timber doors and the vanity unit spanning the opposite wall.

There are subtle correlations between the two sides of the room, so as not to make the upcoming insertion feel disparate. For instance, a glass screen matches the height of the mirror opposite.

The shower also includes a stainless-steel handrail that doubles as a towel rail, matching the rest of the bathroom fixtures.

“The scale of the commission demanded close attention to every decision, from the arrangement of the room to the meeting of two stones,” added Dal Pozzo.

“By revealing the original fabric, retaining what worked and introducing a few carefully resolved elements, we sought to give the clients a bathroom that would serve them into the future and continue the architectural story of their home.”.

Lumeah is shortlisted for bathroom of the year in Dezeen Awards 2026.

Other projects in this category include Kan Atelier’s design for the William King Apartment, a residence in a 1950s block in Athens, which won the public vote.

Photography by Tom Ross.

Sotheby’s makes last-minute deal to sell $180m Van Gogh painting following dispute

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Recent findings suggest that the Sotheby’s statement records that the auction house is “pleased to confirm that an agreement has been reached between the Blaquier-Arrieta family and all of the legal descendants of Hedwig and Samuel Fischer regarding the sale of Vincent van Gogh’s Châtaigniers en fleurs”.
  • It has been revealed that the work is estimated at around $180m ($207m with fees) and has been guaranteed by Sotheby's to sell.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that sotheby’s today unveiled that a settlement has been reached over the sale of Vincent van Gogh’s Blossoming Chestnut Trees (Châtaigniers en fleurs) (May 1890). The work has been poised to achieve a record price for the artist but became the subject of a claim by the heirs of its Jewish former owners, who called for the work to be withdrawn from the 18 November auction in New York.

Recent findings suggest that the Sotheby’s statement records that the auction house is “pleased to confirm that an agreement has been reached between the Blaquier-Arrieta family and all of the legal descendants of Hedwig and Samuel Fischer regarding the sale of Vincent van Gogh’s Châtaigniers en fleurs”. The sale will now proceed as planned.

It has been revealed that the work is estimated at around $180m ($207m with fees) and has been guaranteed by Sotheby's to sell. This is far in excess of the previous record of $117m, paid at Christie’s in 2022 for Van Gogh’s Orchard with Cypresses (April 1888).

The Blaquier-Arrieta family, from Argentina, bought Blossoming Chestnut Trees in 1975. As the Sotheby’s statement explains: “In recognition of the painting’s complex Nazi-era history and the suffering endured by the Fischer family during the Holocaust, the two families have reached a mutually satisfactory resolution and the work will be sold pursuant to their agreement.”.

According to recent reports, the provenance in the Sotheby’s catalogue entry notes, as it has done since last month, that the painting was acquired by the Berlin publisher Samuel Fischer and his wife Hedwig in 1909. Their son-in-law, Gottfried Bermann Fischer, deposited the Van Gogh with the Amsterdam gallery Paul Cassirer in 1932 or 1933—and it was then bought by Paris collectors Henriette and Marcel Kapferer in 1936.

Industry observers note that last Thursday (12 November), in a surprise move, the Berlin-based restitution researcher Gunnar Schnabel sent a letter to Sotheby’s, on behalf of the Fischer heirs. He questioned the 1936 sale—which he says took place three months after the family had left Berlin for Vienna—asking Sotheby’s to prove that the picture had been sold at its market value and that its sale was not forced. In the meantime, Schnabel asked for this week’s sale to be delayed.

In a statement, the Fischer heirs commented: “We are grateful for the trusting and fair negotiation and collaboration with Sotheby’s and the Blaquier-Arrieta family, which make it possible to acknowledge the suffering of the Fischer family during the Nazi era and honour Gisela Berman Fischer's [granddaughter of Samuel and Hedwig] history of seeking justice for her family.”.

The Blaquier-Arrieta family commented: “We are pleased to have reached an amicable resolution with the Fischer heirs. We appreciate the constructive dialogue that made this resolution possible and look forward to an extraordinary result and to passing along this masterpiece to a new generation of collectors.”.

No details have been released on the nature of the agreement and whether the Fischer family will receive financial compensation.

What impact, if any, the short-lived dispute will have on the sale will only become apparent with the bidding.

Jon McCormack, Apple’s head of photography and camera software development, has retired. A spectacular photographer in his own right, McCormack is stepping away, and his departure signals a major change for Apple regardless of the circumstances.

It has been revealed that bloomberg reports that McCormack retired at the end of October. This information has not been independently verified, as at the time of publication, neither Apple nor McCormack has confirmed his departure.

Enhancement 11/20 @ 8 AM: McCormack shared this story on his Instagram, perhaps subtly confirming its accuracy.

Industry observers note that mcCormack, who was Apple’s vice president of camera and photo engineering, has been a major figure at the Silicon Valley giant since he arrived there in 2018. He oversaw the development of not only the iPhone camera system but also the camera software and all of the computational features that go along with it.

It has been revealed that he was present for every briefing and discussion about the iPhone camera system through that time and became personally known to everyone at PetaPixel. He is also regularly quoted speaking about Apple’s philosophy regarding cameras and photography.

“Here’s our view of what a photograph is: The way we like to think of it is that it’s a personal celebration of something that really, actually happened,” he told PetaPixel back in 2024, just as generative AI was beginning its steady march into the creative industry. Apple has, since then, largely stayed that course.

Recent findings suggest that perhaps most importantly, McCormack is actually a photographer. In April, PetaPixel featured his most recent book, titled “Patterns: Art of the Natural World.”.

It has been revealed that “I grew up on a farm in the Outback, Queensland in Australia,” McCormack stated. “Sheep and cattle property. We had no full-time electricity. We had a 32-volt generator that dad would run at night so that a little 12-inch black and white TV could be a thing. This is also when I got my first camera, my hand-me-down camera, and it wasn’t even my dad’s hand-me-down camera. It was my grandfather’s, a Minolta 35mm Mark IV made in either 1949 or 1950. I still have it.”.

His series made it abundantly clear that McCormack cares deeply about nature.

“My goal here is for people to look at our planet like a Fabergé egg,” McCormack explained. “It is unique, one of them in existence. It’s fragile, it’s intricate, it’s beautiful. It’s something to be protected and taken care of, and it’s something you can fall in love with.”.

In a recent development, it’s hard to think of a greater loss for Apple than McCormack. It is unlikely that Apple will find someone who is nearly as talented or who cares as much about photography as a fine art. PetaPixel is hard-pressed to believe there was anyone better for his role at the company than he was.

B2 Architecture turns North Korean defector testimonies into Prague exhibition

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • B2 Architecture has created the Life Behind the Walls exhibition in Prague, using a maze of red timber frames and translucent fabric to explore life in North Korea.
  • The 1,500-square-metre exhibition takes visitors from a bright, interactive installation designed around a children’s book to a darkened gallery featuring portraits and testimonies from North Korean defectors.
  • It has been revealed that B2 Architecture divided the installation into two contrasting environments.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photography by Radek Šrettr Úlehla.

B2 Architecture has created the Life Behind the Walls exhibition in Prague, using a maze of red timber frames and translucent fabric to explore life in North Korea.

The 1,500-square-metre exhibition takes visitors from a bright, interactive installation designed around a children’s book to a darkened gallery featuring portraits and testimonies from North Korean defectors.

It has been revealed that B2 Architecture divided the installation into two contrasting environments. The first features a grid of red-painted timber beams, with large sheets of red and pink fabric suspended between the frames to create semi-transparent walls.

The structure forms a maze that visitors can explore, with glimpses of other rooms and activities visible through the fabric.

Illustrated panels, games and interactive activities are fitted into the structure, while photographs by photographer Michal Huniewicz show North Korea as it is presented to the outside world.

Children are encouraged to navigate the maze independently and stop to draw, write and complete activities as they move through the installation.

The displays are based on Tota lítá, a children’s book by North Korean studies scholar and writer Nina Špitálníková, which explains the principles of totalitarianism in language that is accessible to younger readers.

Industry observers note that “Children are often given very little space within exhibition formats,” B2 Architecture told Dezeen. “This project consciously challenges that convention.”.

The atmosphere changes as visitors pass between two walls displaying photographs of the border between North Korea and China by photographer Tim Franco.

Beyond this threshold, the playful red maze gives way to a dark gallery. This contains black display structures with portraits and personal accounts of people who escaped North Korea, alongside stories of those who did not survive its regime.

Tall, translucent fabric panels printed with shadowy human figures were arranged throughout the space, creating silhouettes that overlap with the portraits displayed behind them.

In a central room, a monumental statue of North Korean leader Kim Jong Un stands on a raised plinth, surrounded by spotlights and theatrical mist.

The temporary installation was constructed using lightweight, modular timber beams and stretched textiles, allowing it to be assembled and dismantled efficiently.

The timber structure was retained for use in another project, while the textiles and flooring were passed on to several theatres for reuse.

Prague-based B2 Architecture was founded by architect Barbara Bencová in 2012 and works across residential and commercial architecture, interiors and public spaces.

Other projects by the studio featured on Dezeen include the DDB Prague office, which features an anamorphic optical illusion that makes the advertising agency’s logo appear complete from a particular viewpoint.

Photography by Radek Šrettr Úlehla.

It weighs 1.85 pounds and comes with a skirt that controls where the light spills and a storage bag. It attaches to lights with a Bowens mount, a bayonet fitting common on studio lights. The RC 100B and RC 60B do not have that mount, and SmallRig’s listings say they need the company’s Bowens mount adapter, sold separately, to use a softbox like this one.

Industry observers note that two lights are aimed at close-up work. The RM 03 is a bendable light for macro, or close-up, photography that SmallRig designed for subjects such as mushrooms, plants, and insects. It can wrap around a tree trunk, attach with its clamp, or stand on ground stakes, and it is rated IP54 against rain and dust. It is $39.99, down from $49.99. The RM01 kit is a 2.2-ounce light that SmallRig rates as waterproof. It comes with eight color filters, a diffuser, and a barn door, a set of flaps that narrows the beam. SmallRig suggests it for toy photography, stop motion, and macro. It is $31.99, down from $39.99. Both are 20% off.

Three zoomable flashlights are built to put colored or patterned light on a subject or a background. Each comes with gobos, patterned inserts that shape the beam. The RF 05B produces white light that adjusts from a warm 1900K to a cool 8000K. It weighs 7.6 ounces, is rated IP65 against rain and dust, and costs $31.99, down 20% from $39.99. The 10-watt RF 10C has LEDs in four colors (orange, blue, white, and red) and runs about three hours at full power, according to SmallRig. It drops to $39.99 from $49.99, also 20% off. The 20-watt RF 20C has five colors, and SmallRig suggests it for background and rim lighting, a light from behind that outlines the subject, in portraits at weddings and conventions. It is $67.99, down 15% from $79.99.

It has been revealed that the universal phone cage kit, a frame with two side handles for handheld filming, is $47.99, reduced 20% from $59.99. SmallRig says the two handles add stability for moving shots, and the aluminum cage has mounting points for a microphone and a light. The All-in-One kit comes with an LED light and a microphone, plus a tripod and a power bank holder, and its handles rotate from the sides to the top. SmallRig says it fits phones from 2.52 to 3.46 inches wide. It is $161.49, down 15% from $189.99.

The selfie monitor kit lets someone filming alone see the frame while using the phone’s rear camera. Its small monitor mirrors the phone’s screen wirelessly from up to 32.8 feet, and a wireless remote triggers the camera. It is $51.99, a 20% discount from $64.99. Read the listing before ordering: SmallRig says the kit is not suitable for Google Pixel phones or the Samsung S22 series, and that with the iPhone’s own camera app it supports 1080p at 60 frames per second, not 4K at 60.

For filters, the 5-in-1 magnetic 67mm kit is $95.99, down 20% from $119.99. Its three filters attach magnetically, so they swap quickly: a variable ND filter, which darkens the image by an adjustable amount; a circular polarizer, which cuts glare and reflections; and a Black Mist 1/4 filter, which softens highlights. The kit also includes a threaded ring that puts the same filters on a camera lens with a 67mm filter thread. On a phone it needs one of SmallRig’s phone cages and a filter ring that is sold separately, so check the listing for the cage models it fits.

In a recent development, smallRig’s Cage for DJI Osmo Action 6 (Advanced Edition) is a 2.4-ounce aluminum frame with a cold shoe, a slot for mounting a small light or microphone. It snaps on without tools, and SmallRig claims the battery can be changed without taking the cage off. A lens cover and a wrist strap are included. It is $31.99, down 20% from $39.99.

It has been revealed that four accessories for DJI’s Osmo Pocket cameras are discounted, and fit differs by model. The auto-deploy mini tripod has the lowest price on the list at $14.44, 15% off $16.99. Its legs open on their own when it is set down, and they are magnetic. SmallRig claims they can hold up to 0.66 pounds on a refrigerator or another surface a magnet sticks to. The magnetic desktop stand tilts and has a magnetic back, a cold shoe, and a plate that fits Arca-type tripod clamps, a common quick-release standard. It is $27.99, down 20% from $34.99. SmallRig lists both for the Pocket 4P, Pocket 4, and Pocket 3. The mini tripod attaches with a standard 1/4-inch screw, which its listing pairs with the Pocket 4 and Pocket 3 handle, so check the mount on a Pocket 4P before ordering.

Two filter kits are listed for the Pocket 4P only. The ND16, ND64, and ND256 kit, which also includes a polarizer and a Black Mist filter, is $39.99, down 20% from $49.99. The variable ND kit is $33.14, reduced 15% from $38.99. ND, or neutral density, filters cut the light reaching the sensor so video can keep a slower shutter speed in bright conditions. The first kit has three fixed strengths that cut four, six, and eight stops of light, and each stop halves the light. The variable filter adjusts from one to five stops for changing conditions. SmallRig claims neither kit interferes with the gimbal’s rotation or darkens the corners of the frame.

According to recent reports, A cage is a metal frame that wraps a camera body and adds threaded holes for handles, monitors, and microphones. Each is built for one camera model, so match the model name on the listing to the camera.

For the Sony FX5, four HawkLock cages and kits are 20% off. HawkLock is SmallRig’s name for a mounting rail that accessories such as handles slide onto and lock by themselves. The cage on its own is $71.99, down from $89.99, and has a clamp that keeps an HDMI cable from pulling out of the camera. The Advanced HawkLock cage is $95.99, down from $119.99, and SmallRig claims its base slides straight into Arca-type tripod clamps and the DJI RS gimbals named on the listing, for quick moves between tripod, gimbal, and handheld shooting.

It has been revealed that the kit for the FX5 and its XLR handle has a closed-ring extension that SmallRig indicates improves the grip of Sony’s XLR top handle, plus a wrist strap, and is $111.99, down from $139.99. The kit with a top handle and wrist strap has an enclosed top handle that SmallRig says helps prevent drops during low-angle shots. It is $127.99, down from $159.99. XLR is the connector type used by professional microphones. One caution from the listings: the top plate has to come off the cage before Sony’s XLR handle or viewfinder is mounted.

Recent findings suggest that three Nikon accessories round out the list, each 20% off. The Z6 III cage, $55.99, down from $69.99, locks to the camera at three points, which SmallRig claims stops it from twisting, and its base fits Arca-type tripod clamps and the DJI RS gimbals named on the listing. The ZR cage, $43.99, down from $54.99, has a silicone grip and a clamp that holds HDMI and USB-C cables in place. The L-shaped handgrip for the Z f is a 3.6-ounce silicone grip that SmallRig says gives the camera a more secure hold. It attaches with a thumbscrew, no tools needed, and has a quick-release plate for Arca-type tripod clamps. It is $31.99, down from $39.99.

In a recent development, the SmallRig S70 Ultra-Thin Wireless Microphone has the deepest discount in the sale: 40% off at $53.99, down from $89.99, a saving of $36. SmallRig designed it for content creators, vloggers, and filmmakers who want to record audio without a bulky microphone setup, and claims its thin, discreet design suits interviews, talking-head videos, and on-the-go recording, where keeping the microphone out of sight matters.

Recent findings suggest that the sale ends November 30, 2026. SmallRig is running the sale at its Amazon U.S. store, the SmallRig official store, and B&H. The prices in this article are the ones SmallRig supplied for Amazon U.S., and the other two stores may differ. The company also notes that prices and availability may change during the promotion, so check each product page for the current price and stock.

Branding: Zero 10 brand identity by Saffron

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (451 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Abduzeedo

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Saffron builds the Zero 10 brand identity for Art Basel from Malevich's 1915 0,10 show, a frame-like mark for digital art.
  • It has been revealed that the mark itself does almost nothing, and that is the point.
  • Industry observers note that the type is a heavy geometric sans, set large enough that single words carry a whole poster.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Saffron builds the Zero 10 brand identity for Art Basel from Malevich's 1915 0,10 show, a frame-like mark for digital art.

It has been revealed that the mark itself does almost nothing, and that is the point. Two numerals, a round zero and a straight ten, sit far apart, open space held between them. The space is the frame: whatever sits inside it, a glowing orb, black liquid, purple fur, becomes the artwork, while the numerals stay fixed at the edges. On deep magenta, the word Future fills the width in cream capitals under a small 0 10. On black, Art creators does the same work over silver bubbles. The system frames the art, labels it, and gets out of the way.

Industry observers note that the type is a heavy geometric sans, set large enough that single words carry a whole poster. Future, Art creators, and The collectors each run at a scale where the letterforms read as shapes first and words second, with the small 0 10 lockup above them. Every layout follows the same grid: mark at the top, one headline in the middle, the Art Basel wordmark anchored low, and artwork inset in a free corner.

Sources indicate that spacing does as much work as the letters. The open gap between zero and ten is protected in every lockup, and the headlines sit on broad magenta, black, or pale blue fields. Even the flags keep the discipline: one black flag carries the numerals running down its length, the next the Art Basel wordmark, so the pair reads as one system at a distance.

In a recent development, the identity lives on fabric, glass, and screens. Four flags run the system against a flat blue sky: purple pixel weave, black with the white numerals, soft pink, and black with the Art Basel wordmark. At the fair, the mark frames vast LED walls of particle fields and glitch color. The platform debuted at Art Basel Miami Beach, where Saffron claims the first preview day alone brought seven-figure blue-chip sales, with several collections sold out.

Recent findings suggest that saffron built the launch as a toolkit as much as a look, with messaging for every stage of the journey, to attract, educate, and convert new audiences. The name travels: Zero 10 reads the same in any language, and the platform now runs across Art Basel's global fairs. Some case-study imagery was generated with AI, Saffron notes. Art Basel chief executive Noah Horowitz says the partnership "gave us the creative space to experiment and the insight to build a platform that deeply engages our community with absolute authenticity.".

See the full Zero 10 case study from Saffron.

#91684. Industry News: Eight highlights from this year's Sharjah Architecture Triennial

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1403 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dezeen ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: Eight highlights from this year's Sharjah Architecture Triennial

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1403 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dezeen

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The third Sharjah Architecture Triennial focuses on the myriad ways architecture can be understood through the lens of anthropology.
  • Curated by anthropologist Vyjayanthi Rao, this year’s edition was centred on the theme Architecture Otherwise: Building Civic Infrastructure for Collective Futures.
  • Rao noted the 2026 Sharjah Architecture Triennial, which takes place over five months, will invite discourse about the different ways cities and urban life can be imagined.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The third Sharjah Architecture Triennial focuses on the myriad ways architecture can be understood through the lens of anthropology. Here are our highlights from the event, including installations and exhibitions.

Curated by anthropologist Vyjayanthi Rao, this year’s edition was centred on the theme Architecture Otherwise: Building Civic Infrastructure for Collective Futures.

Rao noted the 2026 Sharjah Architecture Triennial, which takes place over five months, will invite discourse about the different ways cities and urban life can be imagined.

“Though I’m not an architect, I’m literally talking to students day in and day out about how they see the world, and how that translates into the practice,” Rao told Dezeen.

“Being an academic, you’re always asked to define yourself in terms of your discipline,” she continued. “It doesn’t make sense to limit yourself, especially when you are in the practice of life.”.

“You’re learning from people about the ways in which they live – that’s what I do as an anthropologist, and I think that’s what a lot of architects do because they’re inspired to build for people and the places that they inhabit and thrive in.”.

Read on for eight highlights from this year’s Sharjah Architecture Triennial.

Open the School by Curry J Hackett.

Artist Curry J Hackett created this draping shelter spanning the width of the Old Al Jubail Vegetable Market in homage to the Black community in Virginia’s Prince Edward County, which created improvised learning spaces when schools closed during the Civil Rights Movement.

Videos play in the former stalls at either end of the fabric enclosure, screening archival images of the period, as well as images of Rosenwald Schools – the community-building initiative that established thousands of schools for Black children in the South.

In a recent development, “Rather than integrate, schools closed for five years, and leading up to that, schools were dealing with a lot of overcrowding,” Hackett told Dezeen. “The county begrudgingly funded ‘tar paper shacks’, which were shoddy, demoralising structures, to ease overcrowding, and that’s what you’re seeing interpreted here,” he continued.

“Interspersed sonically and visually throughout the installation is a mashing up of the local story of my home town in Virginia with the regional story of the Rosenwald Schools in the South – their architectural rethinking of materials and retelling the history.”.

Research and construction studio Abari showcased a tent-like structure made from a bamboo frame, which was limited in size due to difficulties with material regulations.

The structure is one module of a larger pavilion that was constructed in Nepal, designed as a travelling venue to host bamboo weaving workshops.

“We were not able to create an installation here in the UAE, partly because Abari’s work is based on building with bamboo, and the difficulty with this project was that the global supply chain and its regulations could not be met within the timeframe,” remarked Rao.

“What you see here is one repeatable module of a pavilion that is presently moving within different communities in Nepal – we improvised and decided Sharjah would travel to Nepal, and we’d just have a piece of it here in this exhibition.”.

Sabeel Negotiated by Samar Halloum.

Drawing upon her fieldwork in Sharjah, Palestinian architect Samar Halloum designed a brick pavilion that was shaded overhead by a draping fabric canopy.

In reference to the historical public drinking-water structures in the Gulf region, Sabeel Negotiated features a water fountain and wooden stools for people to gather around.

According to Rao, the strikes by Iran on countries in the Middle East in February disrupted brick supply in the United Arab Emirates, so Halloum redesigned the pavilion with cloth-filled bricks.

According to recent reports, “One of the shortages was bricks because they come from Saudi Arabia, and the factory stopped producing bricks,” stated Rao. “There were some leftover bales of cloth from another installation, so Halloum used those bales and cast them in resin, so you’ll see some of the bricks in the installation are actually made of cloth.”.

History as Repair: Documenting Karachi by Kishwar Rizvi.

This exhibition by art historian Kishwar Rizvi explores how colonised communities in Karachi, Pakistan, took ownership of their urban environment by adapting architectural styles, from European classicism to Mughal-inspired ornament.

Through maps, photographs, sketches and interviews, it aims to shine a light on an architectural history at risk of being forgotten.

The exhibition argues for the protection of colonial-era buildings in Karachi, which are under threat of demolition due to neglect.

Patch-Time by Hiba Bou Akar, Mohamad Hafeda and Nathalie Harb.

The Patch-Time installation is a collaboration between architect Hiba Bou Akar and artists Mohamad Hafeda and Nathalie Harb that explores the displacement of people in Lebanon, from the 1970s to the present day, through the materials used to protect and repair homes.

In workshops organised by the Patch-Time team with Lebanese non-profit Ahla Fawda, displaced women crocheted tarpaulin, sand-bag cloth and sheeting into panels that form a canopy displayed in a courtyard at the triennial’s Al Qasimiyah School venue.

Underneath the canopy, a table made from breeze blocks, wood and a central mirror displays fabric artwork and the stories of women and children affected by war.

In a recent development, “We worked on two levels: one that is the collective, and one that is more of the individual, looking at how people shelter their home through war adversity and displacement,” said Harb. “We asked [the women] what their relationship to their home was, and in the pieces, you see how it changes from generation to generation with their relationship to material.”.

After Night There is Nothing by Mohamad Nahleh and Ozayr Saloojee.

Architect Mohamad Nahleh and architecture professor Ozayr Saloojee designed a giant globe of the night sky and split it into three parts, which were scattered across different locations at the triennale.

The outer shells of the curved structures are wrapped in thatch, while the interiors feature vinyl surfaces with designs showing man-made military objects in the sky reimagined as creature-like constellations.

It has been revealed that “This is ‘night sky optimism’ – optimism through catastrophe,” said Nahleh. “The night sky we are talking about in this project is not the sky of beautiful stars and constellations, but the contemporary sky filled with drones, satellites, rockets and missiles that are changing the way we understand the sky above us.”.

According to recent reports, “We have noticed in our research that, especially in geographies witnessing prolonged violence, these objects are producing newly introduced mythical creatures,” he continued. “We think of these creatures as ones that attempt to tame the military brightness that is populating the sky around us.”.

As the Sun Rests by Badriyah Alsalem.

Kuwaiti designer Badriyah Alsalem plotted 41 medieval Arabic poetic names for the sun as cut-outs on the astronomical graph that forms a circular canopy over her pavilion, As the Sun Rests.

Forming patterns of shadow in the sand below, three of the suns were embroidered in red, depicting the sharaq rising sun, saqa’a noon sun and gharab setting sun, while markers on the ground show where these canopy highlights will fall on different dates during the triennial.

“If you look up, you see the static data visualisation, and if you look down, it is animated by the sun itself, so it becomes an analogue device to read this historical data,” mentioned Alsalem.

Lalla Alwyia Khalwa by Ziad Jamaleddine, Makram el Kadi, Iheb Guermazi and Beya Othmani.

Situated on Sharjah’s Al Khan Open Beach, Lalla Alwyia Khalwa is an installation designed as a place for reflection away from the busy city, dedicated to the saint Lalla Alwyia Kasserine.

Dried plants form a grid of columns on a raised platform for visitors to walk through. Stone slabs on the floor mark places of pause, and a metal stool provides a reflective space to listen to the accompanying sound installation.

“We chose the beach because it is already a space for retreat, so this is a retreat inside a retreat,” mentioned the design team, Ziad Jamaleddine, Makram el Kadi, Iheb Guermazi and Beya Othmani.

“We carved a series of spaces – one for prayer, one for sitting, and a courtyard to enjoy the sky.”.

Recent findings suggest that sharjah Architecture Triennial 2026 takes place from 14 November 2026 to 14 April 2027 at various locations across Sharjah, UAE. See Dezeen Events Guide for an up-to-date list of architecture and design events taking place around the world.

Heipi’s Hybrid Tripod Head Quickly Swaps Between Ball, Fluid, and Gimbal Head Modes

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that with more creators capturing both photos and videos, accessory makers are stepping up to meet the demand.
  • Industry observers note that photographers often like ball heads because they are versatile, easy to adjust, and stable.
  • In a recent development, “Today, the line between photography and videography is becoming increasingly blurred.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that with more creators capturing both photos and videos, accessory makers are stepping up to meet the demand. Heipi’s upcoming 2-in-1 hybrid tripod head for photo and video promises the best of both worlds.

Industry observers note that photographers often like ball heads because they are versatile, easy to adjust, and stable. By loosening the head, photographers can promptly recompose their shots. However, ball heads are not as easy to control or as smooth for panning motion as a traditional pan-tilt fluid head, which videographers typically prefer. Further, Heipi states its new head also delivers the balancing performance of a gimbal head, a popular choice for wildlife and birding photographers with huge, heavy lenses.

In a recent development, “Today, the line between photography and videography is becoming increasingly blurred. During a single shoot, creators may switch between wide-angle and telephoto lenses, move from still photography to video, and capture a wider range of perspectives and moments,” Heipi writes on Kickstarter. “Yet different shooting needs often call for different support equipment: a ball head, a gimbal head, a fluid head, and more. Carrying multiple heads adds bulk to your gear and extra weight to every journey.”.

Heipi believes its upcoming hybrid head offers all the benefits of separate tripod heads in a single package.

Recent findings suggest that the Heipi KB50 2-in-1 Hybrid Head weighs 560 grams (just over 1.2 pounds) and is about the size of a traditional ball head. However, it can instantly switch from ball head mode to pan-tilt mode, and videographers can screw on a grip for even more control.

In a recent development, heipi’s latest tripod head also features a stepless counterbalance system designed for gear weighing from 1.5 to 5 kilograms (3.3 to 11 pounds). That encompasses a wide range of equipment, including those substantial, heavy supertelephoto lenses mentioned earlier.

The KB50 features a standard 3/8″-16 UNC female thread on its base, allowing it to attach to a wide variety of tripod legs. It also includes an Arca-Swiss clamp.

The Heipi KB50 2-in-1 Hybrid Head is available to back on Kickstarter now, starting at $428, which is a $120 discount compared to the $548 MSRP. Heipi indicates it will begin shipping in April 2027. With just over 40 days left in the campaign, Heipi has already shattered its $10,000 goal.

Industry News: Casa Mouda opens Lagos gallery to promote design in Nigeria

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Papa Omotayo, Gemma Sfeir and Nifemi Marcus-Bello have helped design two spaces in Lagos for the local creative studio Casa Mouda to host exhibitions that promote design in West Africa.
  • Casa Mouda’s initiative includes the launch of an exhibition to mark the opening of two spaces in Lagos – aiMe Gallery at Eko Hotel and aiMe Concept on Eko Atlantic.
  • AiMe Gallery was redesigned by Lagos-based architect Omotayo at the entrance to the hotel’s conference centre, while aiMe Concept was designed with interior designer Sfeir and designer Marcus-Bello in a storefront in the larger Eko Atlantic development.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Papa Omotayo, Gemma Sfeir and Nifemi Marcus-Bello have helped design two spaces in Lagos for the local creative studio Casa Mouda to host exhibitions that promote design in West Africa.

Casa Mouda’s initiative includes the launch of an exhibition to mark the opening of two spaces in Lagos – aiMe Gallery at Eko Hotel and aiMe Concept on Eko Atlantic.

AiMe Gallery was redesigned by Lagos-based architect Omotayo at the entrance to the hotel’s conference centre, while aiMe Concept was designed with interior designer Sfeir and designer Marcus-Bello in a storefront in the larger Eko Atlantic development.

Both spaces feature exposed concrete walls and columns with touches of warmth, including an earthen bar and screen in aiMe Gallery.

Casa Mouda founder Caline Chagoury Moudaber stated that the spaces, together, were designed to highlight the work done by designers in Lagos.

“As we began to conceive our first chapter of Casa Mouda, we knew we needed to start by recognizing some of the people who had already built so much of its foundation,” noted Chagoury Moudaber.

“There are incredible designers producing on the continent that have done extraordinary work, often taking on alone what usually takes an entire industry elsewhere.”.

The inaugural exhibitions include designers from Lagos, but also those who have chosen to work in the city from abroad.

Among the latter group is American designer Germane Barnes, who showcased his wooden Corona Chair, which features inverted pyramidal legs, and his take on a peacock chair, both produced in Lagos in collaboration with Casa Mouda.

Beyond his contribution to the interior layout, which includes permanent seating for the hospitality at aiMe Concept, Marcus-Bello showcased his LM stools and M2 shelves. The works showcase the production possible in Lagos, but also a more modern, minimalist angle for Marcus-Bello, who is known for his massive metal collectible design pieces.

“Nifemi Marcus-Bello has been quietly doing the legwork to set up real pathways for production for years,” noted Chagoury Moudaber.

On the more craft-oriented side, the collection showcased works in bronze and wood by craftsman Jean Servais Somian, also produced in collaboration with Casa Mouda.

Servais Somian’s work includes an armoire with gridded screen wooden doors, a console with stacked oval shelves, stools in wood with painted recesses that have a graphic appearance and textural cast bronze stools and side tables. It is an impressive array showcasing the craftsman’s range.

French studio Hall Haus showcased its metal basketball hoops and chairs, a blend of African aesthetics with Parisian urban ephemera, reflecting the cross-cultural background of the studio’s members.

Meanwhile, Moroccan designer Hajar Daide showcased a mix of delicate Nigerian woven wood techniques with lush blue Moroccan fabrics for her Friction Bench.

Atmosphere was top of mind for the designers, and Casa Mouda worked with US musician Malloy James to create custom speakers at the entryway for aiMe Gallery, while aiMe Concept features a listening station.

The spaces have also been set up to further promote craft in the region through display and retail, such as textiles, bags and other smaller items such as jewellery.

“The designers who have forged the way are sharing information on what they have learned; the ones new to this area of production are bringing new techniques and perspectives,” mentioned Chagoury Moudaber.

“It has been an incredibly collaborative, generous, and inspiring process – and we are only just beginning.”.

Other recent design showcases include the inaugural Walker Design Triennial in Minnesota and Danish design initiative The Mindcraft Project, curated by Christian + Jade.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Associated Press is moving eight photo editor positions to India today, in a move condemned by unions.

The roles are presently carried out in the United States, but today is their last day. The offshoring follows similar moves this summer, when AP laid off 20 video production jobs in the U.S. and moved them to its hub in Noida, India.

“AP is at it again,” the AP News Guild wrote on X last week. “The News Media Guild learned Monday that AP will offshore eight photo positions after already gutting its U.S. video production team.”.

In a statement, the News Media Guild president Kimberlee Krusei called AP’s move “union busting.”.

It has been revealed that “Fewer people, fewer communities being covered, and less news. That’s the impact of today’s decision,” claims Krusei. “AP’s newsgathering has gone beyond ‘lean’ to leaving many coverage areas abandoned. The remaining journalists are asked to do the impossible and it reveals.”.

The Guild indicates that far from just picking photos taken by AP photographers, the editors provide direction, guide the photographers, correct essential information, and scrutinize images for alterations.

Industry observers note that “They bring decades of local knowledge, news judgment and connections. They negotiate with outside photographers to buy the rights to photos — a now essential part of covering breaking news.”.

One of the affected photo editors, Pablo Salinas, who is based in New York, says that he went above and beyond in 2019 when he obtained the rights to a shocking photo of a drowned father and daughter lying face down in the Rio Grande River.

Recent findings suggest that “That was a picture that I don’t think any other photo editor would have been able to get,” indicates Salinas. “Because it wasn’t ours, I scoured social media and found it and got in touch with the photographer. And she reluctantly gave us permission to use it.”.

The photo went viral and became part of the story about the border crisis.

“AP benefits from having photo editors that are local to where the news is being produced,” states AP photographer Matt Rourke.

Industry observers note that “It’s a partnership,” adds Salinas. “The kind of partnership you lose when you sacrifice these jobs to save a few dollars.”.

According to recent reports, photo editors are intimately involved in the biggest stories of the day. They might be working closely with local photographers to move hundreds of shots illustrating important election results. Or securing the rights to sensitive images that convey difficult news. AP’s Pablo Salinas went in front of the camera to talk about the partnership that’s lost when news leaders sacrifice jobs like his. Tell the company their valuable work can’t just be done from anywhere at this link: https://t.co/euBigYM1tt.

— AP News Guild (@APNewsGuild) November 12, 2026.

An AP spokesperson tells TheWrap that the agency is respecting and following the collective bargaining agreement.

“This is part of the changes we confirmed over the summer to significantly scale our visual production capabilities at our new hub in Noida, India, where we have added dozens of talented journalists to our global news organization,” the spokesperson claims.

The AP states that its hub in Noida will soon employ nearly 100 video producers and photo editors.

Thypoch has revealed its first autofocus prime lens, the $349 AF 23mm f/1.4 Sculptor for Fujifilm X mount.

As a courtesy, PetaPixel agreed to adjust the publish date to November 20. The content of this story is unchanged.

Sources indicate that with its approximately 35mm equivalent focal length, Thypoch’s first autofocus lens for Fujifilm X mount and first autofocus prime lens period is well-suited to a wide range of photographic applications. The 35mm focal length is a classic one for a reason. It works well for street, landscapes, portraits, and travel, to name a few go-to genres.

Industry observers note that thypoch has long been associated with classically-inspired manual focus lenses, like the Simera 50mm f/1.4 and Ksana 21mm f/3.5. However, the organization’s vibe changed considerably when it rolled out its first autofocus lens, the Voyager 24-50mm f/2.8 for full-frame Sony E-mount cameras.

According to recent reports, the new Thypoch AF 23mm f/1.4 Sculptor is styled much like the Voyager, with diagonal lines and a vintage-inspired yet modern design. Although beauty is subjective, the Sculptor will likely earn a few fans thanks to its handsome looks.

It's ultimately what's on the inside that counts, though. Inside the Sculptor, 12 lens elements are arranged across ten groups, promising edge-to-edge sharpness even at the maximum f/1.4 aperture. A 10-bladed aperture diaphragm sits behind the glass.

In a recent development, the lens is also quite compact, measuring just 71.4 millimeters (2.8 inches) long with a 52mm front filter thread. The lens weighs 283 grams (just under 10 ounces).

In a recent development, the autofocus prime can focus as close as 0.25 meters (0.82 feet), giving a maximum magnification of about 0.13x. It's definitely not a macro lens.

According to recent reports, the Sculptor's most obvious competitor is Fujifilm's own XF 23mm f/1.4 R LM WR lens, which costs $1,049.95. Fujifilm's lens weighs 375 grams (13.2 ounces) and is 77.8 millimeters (3.1 inches) long. Thypoch's new lens is much lighter and more affordable.

Fujifilm XF 23mm f/1.4 R LM WRBuy fresh on B&HFujifilm XF 23mm f/1.4 R LM WRBuy used on KEH.comSigma 23mm f/1.4 DC DN ContemporaryBuy new on B&HSigma 23mm f/1.4 DC DN ContemporaryBuy used on KEH.com.

It weighs 340 grams (12 ounces) and is 76.9 millimeters (three inches) long. Again, heavier than Thypoch's upcoming lens by a decent margin.

Then there's the TTArtisan 23mm f/1.4 lens, which costs just $113.99. There's a big catch, though, as TTArtisan's lens is manual focus only. It is extremely compact, measuring just 40.5 millimeters (1.6 inches) long. It weighs about 230 grams (8.1 ounces).

The Thypoch Sculptor AF 23mm f/1.4 should ship soon. It's available to preorder now for $349. It's the most affordable autofocus-equipped 23mm f/1.4 prime lens for Fujifilm X-mount cameras, and the lightest AF lens of its kind for the system. #91675. Harvard museum returns human remains to Brazil

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (648 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Theartnewspaper ↗ Open Full Page

Harvard museum returns human remains to Brazil

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (648 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theartnewspaper

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Brazilian government held two ceremonies this month to mark the repatriation of the remains of two people of African descent taken from the country in the 19th century.
  • Sources indicate that the repatriation is part of a university initiative launched in 2019 to review historical records related to individuals of African descent from Brazil and the Caribbean islands.
  • The National Museum of the Federal University of Rio de Janeiro (Museu Nacional/UFRJ) received the skull of an adult woman, held at the Peabody Museum since 1870 following its transfer from Harvard’s Museum of Comparative Zoology.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Brazilian government held two ceremonies this month to mark the repatriation of the remains of two people of African descent taken from the country in the 19th century. The remains were transferred from the collection of Harvard University’s Peabody Museum of Archaeology and Ethnology in Cambridge, Massachusetts.

Sources indicate that the repatriation is part of a university initiative launched in 2019 to review historical records related to individuals of African descent from Brazil and the Caribbean islands. The review identified one person who is recorded as having been enslaved, while there is strong evidence that the other was as well.

The National Museum of the Federal University of Rio de Janeiro (Museu Nacional/UFRJ) received the skull of an adult woman, held at the Peabody Museum since 1870 following its transfer from Harvard’s Museum of Comparative Zoology. According to records, it was obtained by Walter Hunnewell, a Harvard graduate who accompanied the naturalist Louis Agassiz on an expedition to Brazil in 1865-66, serving as the mission’s photographer.

The skull was described in the records as the “skull of a negro”, with an accompanying note stating it had been “exhumed in the streets of Rio de Janeiro”, although circumstances surrounding its removal are still under investigation. The remains may have been taken from the Cemitério dos Pretos Novos, a burial ground in Rio used for enslaved Africans who died after arriving in Brazil that operated in the 18th century and early 19th century. The burial ground was rediscovered in 1996 during construction work in the city’s port district.

The Museu Nacional/UFRJ will assume temporary custody of the skull, which will not be publicly displayed nor used for research, reproduction or other purposes. Researchers will undertake further work to establish the woman’s origins before decisions are made about the skull’s final destination.

A ceremony on 11 November at the National Museum of the Federal University of Rio de Janeiro to mark repatriation of the remains of an enslaved woman from the Peabody Museum at Harvard University Courtesy Ministério das Relações Exteriores, Brazil.

“This return represents a historical responsibility for the museum,” Juliana Sayão, the deputy director of the Museu Nacional/UFRJ, noted during the ceremony in Rio on 11 November. “We are confronted with the story of a person whose life was shaped by enslavement and the removal of her body from Brazil. Beyond assuming temporary custody, we are committed to treating this history with respect and responsibility.”.

Brazil’s minister of human rights and citizenship, Janine Mello, noted that the repatriation represents a milestone in acknowledging the historical violence resulting from enslavement. “The repatriation of human remains represents a fundamental step towards recognising the memory, history and dignity of the Black population of our country,” she remarked. “More than a century after they were taken from Brazil, these remains will return to the country to receive the dignified treatment to which they are entitled, in a process built on respect for memory, religious traditions and the communities involved.”.

Meanwhile, the Federal University of Bahia in Salvador received the remains of an enslaved African man of Nagô origin. The man is believed to have participated in the Malê Revolt in Salvador in January 1835, a major uprising led by both enslaved and freed Africans against slavery and religious persecution in Brazil. He was reportedly wounded during the uprising and subsequently died in hospital in Salvador.

Industry observers note that A 2022 report on Harvard’s museum collections documented the presence of thousands of human remains, prompting scrutiny of how they had been collected and studied. Neither the museum nor the university returned The Art Newspaper’s requests for comment.

More than four million enslaved Africans disembarked in Brazil during the transatlantic slave trade, making it the largest destination for the forced migration of Africans across the Atlantic. The country was the last in the Americas to abolish slavery, in 1888.

Breaking: Shisuo Design Office creates "surreal" rural house in China using salvaged steel

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Jiang Deng Lu is a house in rural Anhui designed by Chinese studio Shisuo Design Office using stainless-steel offcuts salvaged from the client’s own factory.
  • Described by Shisuo Design Office as a “surreal rural house”, the compact building is raised partially on stilts to look as though it is floating above its sloped riverside site.
  • It sits beside the client’s ancestral home and serves as both a memorial for his late father and a separate dwelling where his elderly mother can host visiting relatives.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photography by Lv Xiaobin.

Jiang Deng Lu is a house in rural Anhui designed by Chinese studio Shisuo Design Office using stainless-steel offcuts salvaged from the client’s own factory.

Described by Shisuo Design Office as a “surreal rural house”, the compact building is raised partially on stilts to look as though it is floating above its sloped riverside site.

It sits beside the client’s ancestral home and serves as both a memorial for his late father and a separate dwelling where his elderly mother can host visiting relatives.

“The client wanted to build a house beside the old family home, providing a comfortable place for his mother and relatives to gather and share meals during holidays,” Shisuo Design Office told Dezeen.

“But beyond this practical need, there was a deeper emotional connection. The old house was left by his father, while the upcoming one represented his own way of creating new memories for the family,” it continued.

“We hoped the house would bring the family together more often, beyond just festive occasions.”.

Jiang Deng Lu’s proportions were determined by the recycled stainless steel offcuts and unused windows salvaged for the project by the client, who is the owner of a stainless steel factory.

“The building’s geometry was strictly reverse-engineered from these salvaged materials,” mentioned Shisuo Design Office.

“Instead of imposing a predetermined architectural form, we meticulously measured and mapped these specific surplus components. The building’s precise dimensions, roof pitches, and structural envelope were entirely reverse-engineered from this salvaged inventory,” added the studio.

“The resulting structure starkly contrasts the client’s modern, lightweight metal industry with the heavy, rooted legacy of his father’s masonry, translating familial love into a rigorous tectonic language,” the studio noted.

Externally, the house is wrapped in a full stainless-steel facade, which the studio said deliberately contrasts with “traditional rural vernacular”. This is punctured by the salvaged windows, positioned to frame views of the river.

It has a rectangular blueprint, with a balcony that is suspended over the river on one side.

Inside is a living space, which sits raised above a dining area accessed directly from the foyer. A bathroom and shower room sit off this dining space.

Interior finishes are pared-back, with stone flooring and white walls complementing the cool-toned exterior of the home. Wooden furnishings and greenery seen through the windows add warmth to the space.

According to Shisuo Design Office, the highlight of the interior is a nine-metre-long window that cantilevers 2.2 metres outward, providing shelter for the terrace below.

“The most distinctive feature is a nine-metre-long horizontal window facing east, overlooking a grove of trees planted by the client’s late father,” remarked the studio.

“For the client, these trees are more than a landscape; they hold personal memories of his father. We wanted to bring the grove into everyday life, rather than simply frame it as a view.”.

Jiang Deng Lu is shortlisted in the rural house category of the 2026 Dezeen Awards, alongside projects including Casa Plaj by Extrastudio and Hata-Mazanka Guesthouses by YOD Group.

Another house featured on Dezeen with a distinctive metal facade is Bondi House, a two-storey, two-bedroom dwelling by Nick Kent Design in Sydney.

Photography by Lv Xiaobin.
