Dezeen Awards 2026 architecture project of the year revealed

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2801 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dezeen

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A tree-top sauna that punctures its architectural framework with the surrounding woodland has been named Dezeen Awards 2026 architecture project of the year following the announcement of all 19 architecture category winners at a party in London.
  • The 19 winners awarded at the ninth annual Dezeen Awards ceremony are located in 11 different countries, including Canada, France, India, Japan and Mexico.
  • Daichi Silent River Tree Sauna won the project of the year award in the architecture sector, it was also named leisure and wellness project of the year.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A tree-top sauna that punctures its architectural framework with the surrounding woodland has been named Dezeen Awards 2026 architecture project of the year following the announcement of all 19 architecture category winners at a party in London.

The 19 winners awarded at the ninth annual Dezeen Awards ceremony are located in 11 different countries, including Canada, France, India, Japan and Mexico.

Daichi Silent River Tree Sauna won the project of the year award in the architecture sector, it was also named leisure and wellness project of the year.

Leisure and wellness projects win big again.

The judges hailed the biophilic project as “beautifully minimalist with a spiritual touch of the soul”.

“It’s totally fresh, totally innovative, and never seen before,” they added.

The win marks the second consecutive year that the leisure and wellness project of the year has gone on to claim the overall sector title, following Herzog & de Meuron’s win last year.

Silent River Tree Sauna by Daichi.

The winning project of the year was up against category winners including a sprawling brick-clad university building modelled on stepped wells in India, a country house with walls formed of unstabilised rammed earth in the UK and a project featuring an 18-kilometre-long limestone wall that allows wildlife to pass through in Mexico.

A housing project that appears as if emerging from the natural landscape and a viewpoint designed to evoke a giant silver ring left on the burial site of a legendary Viking were also amongst the category winners.

Read more about all the winning architecture projects below:.

Architecture project of the year and leisure and wellness project of the year: Daichi Silent River Tree Sauna by Daichi.

The project is nestled within a forest in Kanagawa, southwest of Tokyo, and forms part of the Daichi Silent River retreat alongside guest cabins and additional sauna spaces.

Leisure and wellness is also about mental health, which this project addresses perfectly.

The idea for the project was to make the trees feel part of the architecture, using them as both supports and the defining feature of the pared-back structure.

“Leisure and wellness is also about mental health, which this project addresses perfectly,” said the master jury.

“It is a building that offers a spiritual connection between humans and nature.”.

House (urban) project of the year: Amami House by Sakai Architects.

Local studio Sakai Architects won urban house of the year for its off-grid home on Amami Ōshima, an island in the Amami archipelago off Japan‘s southern coast.

This house highlights how we can live sustainably on a small footprint, in close relationship to nature.

The design was informed by the region’s traditional materials and crafts and its development was spurred by the increase in extreme weather conditions on the island.

“This house demonstrates how we can live sustainably on a small footprint, in close relationship to nature,” the master jury said.

“In a time of climate crisis, it offers an excellent solution for autonomy of energy, while smartly reinterpreting the arrangement and materials of a traditional Japanese house.”.

House (rural) project of the year: Jiang Deng Lu by Shisuo Design Office.

Shisuo Design Office won rural house of the year for Jiang Deng Lu in Anhui, China.

This project sits very delicately in its context and is beautiful as a result.

The compact building is raised partially on stilts to look as though it is floating above its sloped riverside site and made using stainless-steel offcuts salvaged from the client’s own factory.

“This project sits very delicately in its context and is beautiful as a result,” mentioned the judges.

“Innovative in its use of available materials, the project is highly resolved, with incredible quality of light and generosity of space despite a small footprint.”.

Housing project of the year: La Querola by Ribas & Ribas Arquitectos.

Ribas & Ribas Arquitectos won housing project of the year for La Querola in Ordino, Andorra.

A deliberate provocation against the salami-type housing where repetition is at the core.

Made up of seven irregularly shaped blocks embedded into the sloping valley and clad in locally sourced slate, the building’s facades feature recessed windows and openings revealing outdoor terraces.

The judges commended the development’s trend-bucking design as a “deliberately expressionist project, celebrating forms that are not repeatable”.

It has been revealed that “It’s a deliberate provocation against the salami-type housing where repetition is at the core. It’s unconventional, unique, controversial, and a very strong statement,” they mentioned.

According to recent reports, recently, a fire damaged all seven buildings in the uninhabited development. The project also won its category for the 2026 public vote.

House renovation of the year: Haniyasu House by Aatismo.

Local architecture studio Aatismo won house renovation of the year for Haniyasu House, a home in the coastal town of Kamakura, Japan.

It is aesthetic but also functional, cleverly improving seismic stability.

The project saw the single-storey home, originally built in 1967, stripped back to its timber frame after a typhoon had left it structurally unsound, and boldly characterised with rough walls streaked with clay, soil and metal powders to evoke ceramic glazes.

The judges praised the project’s sensitivity to “the history of both the architecture and its owners”.

“It is aesthetic but also functional, cleverly improving seismic stability,” they added.

House extension of the year: Golmorad by ZAV Architects.

Iranian studio ZAV Architects won house extension of the year for its project featuring a series of overlapping arches shifts in colour from terracotta to blue in Tehran, Iran.

It’s clever and fun, with colours that reveal an intent to enjoy life.

Transforming the residence from a weekend villa into a permanent home, its arched series of overlapping arched roofs appears as if organically growing from the home.

The judges found the extension to be “playful with a sense of freedom,” adding that, “it doesn’t manipulate the old house in any way, but instead seems to organically extend it in a very unpredictable direction.”.

“It’s clever and fun, with colours that reveal an intent to enjoy life,” they stated.

The project also won its category for the 2026 public vote.

Civic project of the year: Zando Central Market by Think Tank Architecture.

French studio Think Tank Architecture won civic project of the year for its geometric brick-and-concrete market in Kinshasa, Democratic Republic of Congo.

A bold and strong project with really interesting architectural moves.

The latest building, with space for 20,000 vendors, replaces a historic market on the same site in the capital that was demolished after insufficient maintenance and an overwhelming number of vendors left it unfit for purpose.

“A bold and strong project with really interesting architectural moves, and a capacity to serve the community in a really large-scale way,” remarked the master jury.

“It has a variety within it to allow a lot of activity to take place, with materials that are simple but sustainable.”.

Cultural project of the year: Ismaili Center Houston by Farshid Moussavi Architecture.

Farshid Moussavi Architects won cultural project of the year for its Ismaili Center in Houston, United States.

A very successful community space that has reinterpreted and reimagined the Ismaili-centric typology in a very contemporary rather than self-referential manner.

The building and its sprawling gardens is the first Ismaili Center in the US and is one of several around the world commissioned by the current Imam, or spiritual leader, of the Shia Ismaili Muslim community to serve as a place of worship and cultural exchange.

The judges praised it as a “very successful community space that has reinterpreted and reimagined the Ismaili-centric typology in a very contemporary rather than self-referential manner”.

“It has a stunning relationship to light, and incredible detailing and materiality,” they added.

Workplace project (small) of the year: Carpenter’s Home by Primary Architects.

Chinese studio Primary Architects won small workplace project of the year for its undulating timber roof-topped studio in Xinyang, China.

The architecture speaks of its function, offering space that cleverly facilitates different activities.

The project, a local carpenter’s studio, was designed by the practice to incorporate the craftsman’s studio, as well as a woodcraft workshop that is also open to the public.

“A beautiful project that goes above and beyond the brief,” commended the judges.

“The architecture speaks of its function, offering space that cleverly facilitates different activities.”.

Workplace project (large) of the year: Florentia Village by Turner Works.

Architecture studio Turner Works won large workplace project of the year for Florentia Village, London.

Well-thought out in terms of programme, layout and use of materials and colour.

The practice transformed an old textile manufacturing site in London’s Harringay Warehouse District into a creative hub that offers flexible workshops, studios and industrial units ranging from 46 to 1,400 square metres, alongside community spaces and a cafe.

The judges praised it as “well-thought out in terms of programme, layout and use of materials and colour,” as well as the buildings being “highly flexible, with spaces designed to reinforce a sense of community”.

The project also won its category for the 2026 public vote.

Education project of the year: Prestige University by Sanjay Puri Architects.

Sanjay Puri Architects won education project of the year for its sprawling brick-clad university building in Indore, India.

In a country with a tradition of beautiful campuses, but where most upcoming constructions are based on western typologies, this one breaks the mould.

Referencing traditional stepped wells found in the country, its defining feature is its 9,000-square-metre walkable roof, which comprises 463 stepped platforms that can be used as individual social spaces or as a singular auditorium for up to 9,000 people.

“This project creates its own universe,” said the master jury.

“In a country with a tradition of beautiful campuses, but where most latest constructions are based on western typologies, this one breaks the mould,” they continued.

“The massing of the roof reduces scale and creates interesting courtyards, creating spaces that feel appropriate for both the place and its climate.”.

The project also won its category for the 2026 public vote.

Heritage project of the year: Olympics Utilities by Chartier-Corbasson Architects.

French studio Chartier-Corbasson Architectes won heritage project of the year for its transformation of a neglected underground passage beneath Paris, France.

It was a joy to see so much love put into a building typology that we might typically consider unimportant.

Located in a passage beneath the Trocadero Gardens, the studio created a public restroom, using an industrial-feeling palette of stainless and weathered steel to highlight its thoughtful, utilitarian design while giving it a fresh purpose.

“It was a joy to see so much love put into a building typology that we might typically consider unimportant,” said the judges.

“The project creates architectural character, while also preserving a connection to 19th-century futuristic architecture. Unusual, but iconic.”.

Hospitality project of the year: Perma by Mold Architects.

Perma by Mold Architects in Serifos, Greece won hospitality project of the year, sponsored by Sanderson.

There is an economy of means in its relationship to the topography, which cleverly reduces the overall footprint.

Comprising five guest houses, the rugged retreat on the island of Serifos was constructed by using material extracted during construction to build much of the retreat itself, rather than removing the hillside and building on top of it.

The judges praised its “striking architecture”, noting it as “very innovative in its programmatic possibilities”.

“There is an economy of means in its relationship to the topography, which cleverly reduces the overall footprint,” they stated.

The project also won its category for the 2026 public vote.

Infrastructure and transport project of the year: Naples Underground Central Station by Miralles Tagliabue EMBT.

Spanish architecture studio EMBT won infrastructure and transport project of the year for Naples Underground Central Station in Italy.

A rich environment to spend time in, not just catch a train.

Contrasting its modernist surroundings with a wavy timber roof, the 10,000-square-metre building was designed to replace a previously understated metro entrance with a new public plaza that felt more integrated with the surrounding city.

The judges commended the project as a “successful urban space, both elegant and spatially interesting.”.

“A rich environment to spend time in, not just catch a train,” they continued. “The use of timber is also impressive.”.

Small project of the year: Ring of Bjólfur by Arkibygg Architects.

Local studios Arkibygg Architects and Esja Architecture won small project of the year for their mountain viewpoint in Seyðisfjörður, Iceland.

A minimal intervention that choreographs the discovery of a landscape in a simple but sophisticated way.

Designed to evoke a giant silver ring left on the alleged burial site of a legendary Viking, the viewpoint improves access to a ridge on Mount Bjólfur and celebrates its varied views over the town, valley and surrounding peaks.

The master jury hailed the viewpoint as a “minimal intervention that choreographs the discovery of a landscape in a simple but sophisticated way,” adding that, “the minimal use of material maximises the experience”.

Mixed-use project of the year: York Minster Centre of Excellence by Tonkin Liu.

Architecture studio Tonkin Liu won mixed-use project of the year for its two timber buildings on either side of a Grade I-listed Gothic cathedral in York, United Kingdom.

The materiality speaks to the programming of the building, inspiring a upcoming generation of makers using the space.

Named The Centre of Excellence for Heritage Craft Skills, the buildings include the rectangular Heritage Quad and the triangular Technology Hub, both of which give working stonemasons views of the historic York Minster cathedral.

“There is a real honesty in the combination of buildings, with a unique roofing structure,” said the judges.

“The materiality speaks to the programming of the building, inspiring a new generation of makers using the space,” they added.

Landscape and urban design of the year: Parque del Jaguar by Colectivo C733.

Mexican studio Colectivo C733 won landscape and urban design of the year for its work across Parque del Jaguar in Tulum, Mexico.

Despite limited budget and materials, the interventions create an intimate experience with the landscape, successfully addressing water scarcity, indigenous planting and flexibility for different community projects.

The project aims to safeguard one of the region’s important habitats for jaguars, whose movement through the landscape had become disrupted by roads, development and tourism.

It features an 18-kilometre-long limestone wall that allows wildlife to pass through while protecting more than 1,000 hectares of forest, as well as a network of boundaries, access points and visitor facilities intended to protect the animals’ habitat while allowing people to explore the area.

The judges praised the project as “rooted in its context, made for locals as well as tourists,” adding that, “despite limited budget and materials, the interventions create an intimate experience with the landscape, successfully addressing water scarcity, indigenous planting and flexibility for different community projects.”.

Sustainable building of the year: Rammed Earth House by Tuckey Design Studio.

Rammed Earth house by Tuckey Design Studio in Wiltshire, United Kingdom, won sustainable building of the year, sponsored by Michelmersh.

Although large for a two-person house, it is an incredible testbed that could pave the way for more rammed earth architecture in Europe.

Built on the site of a former brickworks, the rural country house was constructed from both the clay underfoot and an aggregate made from crushed demolition waste to form unstabilised rammed earth walls.

As a form of earth construction that is largely untested at such scale in the UK, the judges commended the project as “a radical example of material innovation”.

“Although large for a two-person house, it is an incredible testbed that could pave the way for more rammed earth architecture in Europe,” they said.

The project also won its category for the 2026 public vote.

Sustainable renovation of the year: De Nederlandsche Bank by Mecanoo.

Dutch firm Mecanoo won sustainable renovation of the year for its major renovation of the Netherlands’ central bank in Amsterdam.

An admirable transformation of a brutalist-era building.

The project involved dismantling a 14-storey tower and opening up the former gold vault, seeing a complete retrofit of De Nederlandsche Bank, a 1968 structure that some had described as the nation’s ugliest building.

The renovation was praised as “an admirable transformation of a brutalist-era building,” by the master jury, who also noted its efforts to adapt it to a different use “while also addressing material and energy concerns.”.

Sources indicate that dezeen Awards 2026 in partnership with TrimbleDezeen Awards is the ultimate accolade for architects and designers worldwide. The ninth edition of the annual awards is in partnership with global technology firm Trimble. Through connected hardware and software solutions, Trimble helps designers to transform the way they shape spaces and buildings as well as drive productivity in the process. Trimble’s collaboration with Dezeen Awards demonstrates its ongoing commitment to inspiring and supporting creative excellence across the globe.

#91652. Breaking: Kandinsky record and trove consigned by Jeff Koons buoy Christie’s 20th-century sale in New York

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1296 w)

Breaking: Kandinsky record and trove consigned by Jeff Koons buoy Christie’s 20th-century sale in New York

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1296 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theartnewspaper

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Buoyed by a handful of gems, Christie’s 20th-century evening sale on 17 November in New York racked up $521m, or $627m with fees, underscoring the allure of rare-to-market trophy works.
  • Sources indicate that the hammer total hit the low-side of the $511m-$743m pre-sale estimate (all estimates calculated without fees).
  • Thirty one of the 75 lots offered were backed by third party guarantees and a further five by house guarantees.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Buoyed by a handful of gems, Christie’s 20th-century evening sale on 17 November in New York racked up $521m, or $627m with fees, underscoring the allure of rare-to-market trophy works.

Sources indicate that the hammer total hit the low-side of the $511m-$743m pre-sale estimate (all estimates calculated without fees). The result was a marked improvement on last November’s equivalent sale, which made $390.1m, or $471.7m with fees.

Thirty one of the 75 lots offered were backed by third party guarantees and a further five by house guarantees. Three multi-million dollar offerings were withdrawn from the sale, including an Andy Warhol self portrait, estimated between $14m-$18m.

It wasn’t a perfect evening: six lots failed to sell. These included a small-scale group of seven Jackson Pollock paintings from the 1950s (est $7m-$9m); a 1915 Modigliani painting Beatrice Hastings sitting (est $5m-$7m); and a 1945 Léger canvas (est $1.2m-$1.8m). Including the three withdrawn lots, this amounted to an 88% sell through rate.

Still, six artist records were set, including the 11-ft high Fernando Botero bronze, Horse (2006), which was parked on the sidewalk in front of Christie’s Rockefeller Center headquarters, and made $4.2m ($5.2m with fees).

The marathon evening got off to a modest start with Mary Bauermeister’s wooden box construction packed with optical elements, Nature Mort (1967-69), which made $100,000 ($128,000 with fees), the first from the collection of investment banker and art scholar Herbert Lust.

The Lust trove of eight works (a Frank Stella estimated at $7m-$10m was withdrawn before the sale) realised $42m with fees, topped by Alberto Giacometti’s impossibly thin, 119cm-high bronze, Figure, demie grandeur (no.2) from 1949 that made $22m ($25.9m with fees), against an estimate of $20m-$30m.

Beyond Lust, a late and untitled Mark Rothko acrylic on paper laid down on canvas in fiery red hues from 1968 made $11.5m ($13.9m with fees) and Philip Guston’s feather light brush strokes in Painting from 1952 sold for $3.3m ($4.1m with fees), topping out the few Ab-Ex offerings.

Recent findings suggest that the evening featured two mega-priced lots, both estimated at $60m-$80m. Wassily Kandinsky’s Weimar-era abstraction Betonte Ecken (accentuated corners, 1923), which once owned by the Guggenheim Museum co-founder Hilla Rebay, soared to a record $74m ($85.8m with fees). The anonymous seller acquired it at Sotheby’s Fresh York in May 1986 for $1m.

Gustav Klimt’s dazzling lakeside composition, Litzlbergkeller from 1915-16, was observed and painted by Klimt with the aid of a telescope positioned and capturing the stout likeness of the Austrian inn he frequented for eight idyllic summers. It floated to $71m ($82.3m with fees).

Alex Rotter, Christie’s global president, nabbed both works for anonymous clients on his rainmaking telephone.

The Klimt had been acquired by last night's consignor at Sotheby’s Upcoming York in May 1997 from the estate of Neue Galerie co-founder Serge Sabarsky for a then-record $14.4m.

A standout of the season, Wilfredo Lam’s large, tropical-inspired composition executed in a Magical Realism style, Ogue Orisa (Eggue Orissa, l’herbe des dieux) from 1943, made a record $9.5m ($11.6m with fees). It debuted at the Pierre Matisse Gallery in 1944 and was recently featured in the Museum of Modern Art retrospective Wilfredo Lam: When I Don’t Sleep, I Dream. It last sold at auction at Sotheby’s Latest York in November 1997 for $1.3m with fees. The Lam came to market backed by a third-party guarantee.

Impressionist era paintings were also in rich supply. Paul Cézanne’s luscious tabletop still life Tasse, verre et fruits (around 1877) was consigned by the 86-year-old billionaire businessman William I. Koch. It brought $11.5m ($13.9m with fees).

The Cézanne was once owned by the former Dutch banker Siegfried Kramarsky, whose estate sold Vincent van Gogh’s Portrait of Dr Gachet from 1890 at Christie’s New York in May 1990 for a then-record $82.5m with fees.

Industry observers note that french painting masters continued with Camille Pissarro’s evocative and crowded Parisian cityscape (sans protesters), Le Pont-Neuf, après-midi de pluie, 1re série from 1901 brought $6m ($7.4m with fees). It last sold at Christie’s New York in November 2019 for $6.5m with fees.

Cornelis Cornelisz van Haarlem’s Hercules and Achelous (1590).

Significant name consignors were not in short supply as evidenced by a trove of Picassos and several Old Master works under the marketing title “Heroes & Lovers: Property of a Distinguished Collector”—also known as Jeff Koons.

The group was led by Picasso’s snogging couple, Le Baiser (October 1969), which is famed in part for its inclusion in the artist’s late paintings exhibition in Avignon at the Palais des Papes in 1970, and went for $26.5m ($31.1m with fees).

The monochrome composition depicting the artist and his wife and muse Jacqueline Roque conveys both passion and love in the artist’s last decade. Though a relatively significant price, it came nowhere near its $40-$60m estimate.

Backed by a third-party guarantee, the work was acquired by Koons from Sotheby’s Latest York in May 2008 for $17.4m, the same year his Balloon flower-Magenta from 1995-2000 sold at Christies London for £12.9m, or $25.7m.

According to recent reports, picasso’s Tête de femme (Dora Maar), painted in wartime Paris on 25 May 1941 sold for $25.5m ($30m with fees). Another Dora Maar split-angle composition with her face featured alongside her rival Marie-Therese Walther from 1939-40 brought $6m ($7.4m with fees) against an unrealistic estimate of $10m-$15m.

Sources indicate that the Koons trove, backed by third party guarantees also included a trio of Old Master works, topped by Cornelis Cornelisz van Haarlem’s dramatic, mythological depiction of Hercules and Achelous from 1590, and hugely scaled at 91.45cm by 242.57cm. It brought $11.5m ($13.9m with fees), below its $12m-$18m estimate but enough to once again set the artist's record. Koons acquired it at Christie’s Newly introduced York in April 2008 for a then-record $8.1 million. All in, the Koons group tallied $104.7m with fees.

Willem de Kooning’s rushing Yellow River from 1958, deaccessioned by the Whitney Museum of American Art in New York “to benefit the collection", and once described by the late critic Thomas B. Hess as “abstract parkway landscapes”, made $9m ($11m with fees).

Industry observers note that one of the best back stories of the season came courtesy of Georgia O’Keeffe’s Near Abiquiu, Fresh Mexico I (1930), which was found buried in a trunk by the niece of the East Village owner who received it as a college graduation present in 1963. Rarely does one see property titles from the East Village. One newspaper article mentioned the elderly owner, a former Foreign Service member, decided to hide the painting away in the mid 1980s after one visitor eyed it and she grew suspicious.

Sources indicate that it hasn’t been seen in public since 1931 when it was featured in Alfred Stieglitz’s An American Place gallery solo show of the artist. It made $3.9m ($4.8m with fees).

Another version of the curvy sand hills of the Rio Grande Valley composition where O’Keeffe had her studio sold at Christie’s Newly introduced York in May 2018 from the collection of Peggy and David Rockefeller for $8.4m.

Though the Frida Kahlo painting Congreso de los pueblos por la paz (1952) was withdrawn at the 11th hour over export issues, her husband Diego Rivera fared better, with the floral Vendedora de flores, de Tehauntepec (1929) blossoming at $8.1m ($9.9m with fees). It blew past its $3.5m high estimate—another winner for the William I. Koch collection which all in realised $66.3m.

“It felt like a very calibrated evening with a solid but measured pace,” said Adrien Meyer, Christie’s auctioneer, as he exited the salesroom. “There was significant participation from Asia that I haven’t seen in a while.”.

The evening action resumes Wednesday at Sotheby’s and the awaited offering of a $180m Vincent van Gogh painting Châtaigniers en fleurs from 1890.

DxO Year in Review 2026: Four New Versions and Where Each One Fits in Your Edit

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2863 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Petapixel

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that A lot changed in DxO’s photo editing tools in 2026.
  • Together, DxO’s software updates changed how a hard file gets edited, from first cleanup to finished look.
  • Sources indicate that full disclosureThis article was brought to you by DxO.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that A lot changed in DxO’s photo editing tools in 2026. The strongest noise reduction reached far more cameras. Masks learned to find each person in a frame, and the distance behind them, without a brush. The glow of film around a streetlight went from a stack of layers to a single filter.

Together, DxO’s software updates changed how a hard file gets edited, from first cleanup to finished look.

Sources indicate that full disclosureThis article was brought to you by DxO. DxO’s Black Friday prices apply to latest licenses and upgrades of PhotoLab 10, Nik Collection 9, ViewPoint 6, PureRAW 6 and FilmPack 8 through November 29. The prices are applied automatically at dxo.com/bf26/PetaPixel, with no code required.

Photos taken in Fresh Mexico by Chris Niccolls and Michael Bonocore, in Cuba and Morocco by Michael Bonocore, and the Milky Way by Matt Suess.

DxO released new versions of four applications in 2026: PureRAW 6, Nik Collection 9, PhotoLab 10 and, in October, ViewPoint 6. DxO keeps improving its applications, and three of them received free updates in November.

Sources indicate that each one handles a different stage of an edit. PureRAW cleans the RAW file, the unprocessed data a camera’s sensor records. PhotoLab develops that file into a share-worthy photograph, ViewPoint corrects perspective and distortion, and Nik Collection adds the finishing look.

Recent findings suggest that always looking for new ways to edit old photos, I ran photos from New Mexico, Cuba and Morocco through three of them for PetaPixel stories throughout 2026. Even though I also shoot astrophotography, a fourth story followed OM SYSTEM ambassador Matt Suess through a Milky Way edit, as he is a much more impressive editor than I am. What follows runs in the order of a typical edit of mine, and that starts before any creative decision, with the RAW file itself.

Recent findings suggest that if you zoom to 100% on a frame shot at a high ISO, the camera’s sensitivity setting, the flaws become obvious. There is grainy noise in the shadows, edges the lens left soft and a dust spot or two from the sensor. Every later editing adjustment that you add only makes the problems worse, and they follow the photograph through the rest of the edit.

Recent findings suggest that pureRAW 6 helps to make all of these fixes. It applies noise reduction, lens corrections and dust removal to the RAW file before editing starts, then hands back a latest file to edit. The usual choice for that file is a DNG, a format that keeps a RAW file’s editing flexibility. The original RAW file is never modified.

This year’s PureRAW 6 expanded the reach of DeepPRIME XD3, the stronger of PureRAW’s two noise reduction engines.

Recent findings suggest that in the past, it only worked with Fujifilm’s X-Trans sensors. It now works with Bayer sensors, the design used by Canon, Nikon, Sony and OM SYSTEM.

The lens corrections are an especially strong feature of DxO software, starting with PureRAW. They test each supported camera and lens pairing in their own lab, and PureRAW applies that impressive data for the exact combination that made the photograph.

In this day and age with skyrocketing storage costs, PureRAW 6 shrinks the files with a newly introduced DNG option called High-Fidelity Compression. In one example, a 57.8MB RAW file becomes a 136MB DNG without compression and a 17.2MB DNG with it.

It has been revealed that I have come to find that most photographers are like me, and they often shoot with less than spotless equipment. Luckily, dust spots are automatically detected and removed across a whole batch. And in PureRAW 6, batch edits finish quicker, because the processor prepares the next image while the graphics card renders the current one.

For noise reduction, start with DeepPRIME 3 and switch to XD3 for high-ISO files, heavy crops and fine detail such as feathers and fur. XD3 takes roughly twice as long, though the gap narrows on newer graphics cards, and it can leave artifacts (visible processing errors) on smooth surfaces. For portraits and architecture, stay with DeepPRIME 3.

It has been revealed that if the processed file goes back to Lightroom, make sure to turn off its own lens corrections and noise reduction for that file. PureRAW has already applied both, and running them a second time doubles the correction and creates artifacts.

Recent findings suggest that pureRAW fits a photographer who aims to keep editing in Lightroom, Photoshop or Capture One, because it only changes the file those editors receive. A photographer who would rather work in one application gets DxO’s processing inside PhotoLab 10, the firm’s all-in-one editor. The full walkthrough, with recommended starting values for each control, is in DxO PureRAW 6: The Ultimate Beginner’s Guide.

Brightening one face in a group photograph is a small change. Telling the software which pixels belong to that face is the slow part. The area an adjustment affects is called a mask, and building one by hand means painting an outline and then cleaning up its edges.

PhotoLab 10 builds those masks itself, and my guide shows each one at work on my photographs from Morocco. Its AI Masks recognize the individual people in a photograph instead of treating the group as one subject. One easy step generates a separate mask for each selected person.

For portraits the masks go finer, selecting facial skin, eyes, teeth, lips or facial hair without a hand-painted outline.

No matter the subject matter, every photograph has depth, and the upcoming Depth Masks select areas by how far they are from the camera. PhotoLab builds a depth map, a model of which parts of the scene are near and which are far, without needing depth data recorded in the file.

These masks utilize DxO’s own AI, which runs on the photographer’s own computer, so the masks work on an airplane or in a hotel with unreliable Wi-Fi. Additionally, for those concerned with privacy, this means that the photos are never sent to the cloud and stay local on their computer.

Recent findings suggest that an automatic mask is a starting point to refine. When one misses part of the subject, PhotoLab 10 lets you correct it instead of rebuilding it.

Their U Point technology selects pixels by comparing their color and brightness. The Control Brush applies that matching inside an area the photographer paints.

In a recent development, color grading shifts the color of the shadows, midtones and highlights separately. PhotoLab 10 puts all three on a single wheel, with a Global control for the whole image.

It has been revealed that with the three ranges selected, dragging one marker moves all of them and keeps the same distance between them. This allows for trying a different color direction without rebuilding the color grade.

The free 10.3 update, released in November, extends the masks to noise reduction. Each local adjustment, an edit confined to a masked area, can now use its own noise reduction engine. Reserve DeepPRIME XD3 for the subject, where it extracts the most detail, and let DeepPRIME 3 handle the rest of the frame.

Sources indicate that point a camera up at a building and its walls lean toward each other in the frame. That is a perspective problem, and no exposure or color control fixes it. ViewPoint 6 is the application to fix that: it corrects geometry, perspective and distortion.

Released in October, it adds AI masks to ReShape Fusion, the tool that reshapes part of a picture. A mask finds the outline of a subject, however complex its shape, and the correction mesh is built to match it.

The photographer sets how far the change carries into the rest of the picture. As before, the correction needs no forced crop.

The standalone app now opens RAW files directly. November’s 6.1 update adds DNG export, so a RAW file corrected in ViewPoint can leave with its geometry fixed and continue in any editor that opens DNG files.

According to recent reports, saving and exporting are now separate. Save records the corrections for the next session, and Export produces the finished image.

According to recent reports, photographers miss the days when film made bright lights glow. Light passed through the film’s layers, bounced off the back and leaked in again, leaving a soft halo around streetlights and candle flames. A digital sensor records the same lights with crisp edges and no halo.

Recent findings suggest that rebuilding that glow in Photoshop means duplicating the image, blurring the copy, masking the highlights and blending the layers together. Nik Collection 9 does it with one filter. The suite is a set of plug-ins for Photoshop, Lightroom Classic, Affinity and PhotoLab, and every application in the suite can open the photo from inside one of those editors.

That filter, Halation, is one of three new effects in version 9, each shown on my photographs from Cuba in my Nik Collection 9 guide. It works best on an image that already has strong highlights worth softening, such as a night cityscape or a backlit portrait.

According to recent reports, chromatic Shift copies the color offset of a misaligned printing press, the red edge on one side of a face and the blue-green shadow on the other. A subtle shift of that kind gives a portrait a retro, editorial feel. Using an AI mask can keep it off the eyes and lips.

According to recent reports, glass Effect distorts the frame as if it were shot through textured glass. On a portrait, the distortion can wrap the frame while an AI Object Mask keeps the face sharp.

Recent findings suggest that the upcoming Color Grading filter in Color Efex, one of the Nik Collection 9’s plug-ins, puts shadows, midtones, and highlights on one wheel. Two shortcuts move all three together: one shifts hue, the color the tones lean toward, and the other shifts saturation, how vivid that color is. It gives photographers who finish in Photoshop, Lightroom Classic or Affinity the single-wheel grading that PhotoLab 10 has built in.

Sources indicate that eighteen blending modes now sit inside Color Efex and a second plug-in, Analog Efex. A blending mode sets how an effect mixes with the image beneath it. On the Halation filter, Multiply sinks the glow into the shadows for a darker image, while Soft Light keeps the glow and more of the original contrast.

Aim any of these effects at part of the frame with AI Object Masks and Depth Masks, which work in every plug-in.

Version 9.2, the November update, adds snapshots. A snapshot saves every edit made so far. Try a different look, then come back to the snapshot at any point in the session.

The update also brings 18 upcoming presets, or saved looks: six each for Color Efex, Analog Efex and Silver Efex.

Matt Suess has photographed dark skies for decades and leads astrophotography workshops in places such as Grand Teton National Park. One of the most challenging files he has edited came from a test.

He normally caps his Milky Way exposures at ISO 6400, but he wanted to test PureRAW, so he shot a nightscape at ISO 12,800 to see how far he could push it.

Sources indicate that sharpening or adding contrast to a noisy night file bakes the noise in, so Suess runs noise reduction before he develops the RAW file. He opens PureRAW’s Preview and Process mode, which demonstrates the controls first, because a night sky is where he wants to make those calls himself.

Industry observers note that XD3 is the stronger engine, but a star field is where Suess often skips it. That much processing can start to soften the stars themselves, so he picks DeepPRIME 3, and he treats it as a per-image call.

He keeps Lens Sharpness on Standard, since the Hard setting starts sharpening the noise along with everything else.

The develop pass in Lightroom stays restrained. Suess switches to a color profile built for landscapes in place of the flatter default, adds a little contrast and holds back on the other sliders. He treats this pass as the place to protect the sky’s real color, with the finishing touches saved for later.

The finish happens in the Nik Collection 9 plug-in Color Efex, with the same four filters in the same order on nearly every Milky Way photograph. ClearView lifts the faint gray haze that dulls a night photo, and Suess keeps it low so it does not outline the stars. Glamour Glow spreads a soft bloom of light from the brightest points.

Remove Color Cast pulls one unwanted color out of the frame. Tonal Contrast raises contrast separately in the shadows, midtones and highlights, and he raises the midtones, where the structure of the Milky Way sits. Once the stack works, he saves it as a preset for the next photograph from his astrophotography session.

Suess fine tunes the filters with two tools. A Color Mask, a local adjustment added inside a filter, selects one color across the whole frame. He uses it on air glow, the faint green tint that shows in the sky on very dark nights.

An AI Object Mask points a filter at a single foreground element instead of the whole image.

He judges every move at 100%, not from the small preview. Each one gets a before and after comparison, and he looks for halos, the bright rings that too much contrast leaves around stars. Every step of the edit, with his settings, is in How to Turn a Flat, Noisy RAW Into a Finished Milky Way Photograph.

Some jobs cannot be done by developing a RAW file: a layered composite, added text, an object removed or replaced, detailed retouching. Those jobs need a pixel editor, software that changes the pixels of the picture directly.

DxO announced a partnership with Affinity by Canva in September. Affinity runs on macOS and Windows and costs nothing beyond a free Canva account.

Sources indicate that photoLab 10 launched without a direct Export to Affinity button, and PhotoLab 10.1 added it. With the 10.3 update, Affinity’s own .af files appear in PhotoLab’s library like JPEG and TIFF files.

That makes a round trip possible. A photographer can develop a RAW file in PhotoLab, continue in Affinity with retouching, compositing or layout, then finish and export the result in PhotoLab. Changes saved in Affinity are visible in PhotoLab straight away, and PhotoLab’s own adjustments are stored separately and never change the Affinity document.

Nik Collection 9.2 connects from the other side by saving its work as an .af file. The file keeps the edited image and the original as separate layers, and the masks come across as layers too. Going the other way has a limit: Nik Collection opens an .af file with its layers merged into a single image.

According to recent reports, dxO’s Black Friday prices cover upcoming licenses and upgrades of their five applications through November 29th, 2026. They apply to purchases from dxo.com/bf26/PetaPixel for macOS and Windows, are applied automatically with no code required, and cannot be combined with any other offers.

Sources indicate that pureRAW 6 suits a photographer who wants cleaner files and plans to keep editing in Lightroom, Photoshop or Capture One. It is $99.99, down from $139.99. The upgrade from version 4 or 5 is $69.99, down from $89.99.

Recent findings suggest that photoLab 10 suits a photographer who wants one application for the whole edit, with DxO’s processing, the automatic masks and the Color Grading wheel in the same place. It is $199.99, down from $249.99. The upgrade from version 8 or 9 is $99.99, down from $129.99.

Nik Collection 9 suits a photographer who has an editor already and wants the finishing looks: film glow, color grading and blending modes without stacked layers. It is $149.99, down from $179.99. The upgrade from version 7 or 8 is $79.99, down from $99.99.

In a recent development, viewPoint 6 corrects geometry, perspective and distortion, and version 6, released in October, adds an AI mask that fits a correction to the outline of a subject. It is $99.99, down from $129.99. The upgrade from version 5 is $69.99, down from $84.99.

Sources indicate that filmPack 8 recreates the look of classic film stocks from laboratory measurements of real film, and it includes a tool that prepares home-scanned negatives and slides for editing. It is $74.99, down from $149.99. The upgrade from version 7 is $49.99, down from $89.99.

Industry observers note that free trials of every DxO application are available from dxo.com. November’s 10.3, 9.2 and 6.1 updates are free for owners of PhotoLab 10, Nik Collection 9 and ViewPoint 6.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Dezeen has revealed the six winners of Dezeen Awards 2026 Designers of the Year at this evening’s ceremony in London, which include Lina Ghotmeh, Keiji Ashizawa and Yinka Ilori.
  • Our Designers of the Year awards recognise the best emerging and established talent whose innovative work has made a notable impact on the industry across architecture, interiors and design.
  • This year, Ghotmeh took home the architect of the year award, while studio duo Shohei Kuma and Elsa Escobedo were named emerging architect of the year.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Dezeen has revealed the six winners of Dezeen Awards 2026 Designers of the Year at this evening’s ceremony in London, which include Lina Ghotmeh, Keiji Ashizawa and Yinka Ilori.

Our Designers of the Year awards recognise the best emerging and established talent whose innovative work has made a notable impact on the industry across architecture, interiors and design.

This year, Ghotmeh took home the architect of the year award, while studio duo Shohei Kuma and Elsa Escobedo were named emerging architect of the year.

Interior designer of the year was awarded to Tokyo-based Ashizawa, and Australian designer Yasmine Ghoniem was named emerging interior designer of the year.

London-based Ilori won designer of the year with Stockholm-based Simon Skinner named emerging designer of the year.

Read more about the Designers of the Year below:.

Her poetic approach to materials, memory and landscape brings buildings to life with a rare sensitivity to people, place and planet.

Architect of the year: Lina Ghotmeh.

Industry observers note that ghotmeh, who is the founder of architecture practice Lina Ghotmeh Architecture, is one of the world’s most sought-after architects. Among her high-profile projects was the 2023 Serpentine Pavilion and she was recently appointed to renovate the British Museum’s Western Range galleries.

“From Beirut to Paris and beyond, Lina Ghotmeh creates architecture that feels both rooted in history and entirely of the future,” mentioned the judges.

It has been revealed that “Her poetic approach to materials, memory and landscape brings buildings to life with a rare sensitivity to people, place and planet. We anticipate her studio continuing to go from strength to strength.”.

According to recent reports, ghotmeh is known for her sustainable and historically rooted designs, including the Stone Garden apartment block in Beruit, which was named architecture project of the year at Dezeen Awards 2021. She has received multiple accolades, including being named on the Time100 Next list in 2025 and winning the 2023 Great Arab Minds Award.

Working between Japan and Europe, Kuma and Elsa are creating an architectural vocabulary that feels both regionally distinctive and deeply connected to its surroundings.

Emerging architect of the year: Shohei Kuma and Elsa Escobedo.

Founded by Japanese architect Shohei Kuma and French‑Spanish architect and urban designer Elsa Escobedo, Kuma&Elsa is an emerging architecture studio with offices in France, Spain and Japan.

“Shohei Kuma and Elsa Escobedo’s emerging practice brings a fresh sense of curiosity to architecture, balancing bold forms and material experimentation with tactility and unexpected gestures,” said the judges.

“Working between Japan and Europe, Kuma and Elsa are creating an architectural vocabulary that feels both regionally distinctive and deeply connected to its surroundings.”.

Among the studio’s varied and intriguing work is Nakano House in Japan’s Fukuoka prefecture – an apartment block informed by the design of a traditional Japanese engawa.

His distinct spaces reveal the beauty in restraint, proving that the most powerful interiors are often those that will quietly stand the test of time.

Interior designer of the year: Keiji Ashizawa.

It has been revealed that interior designer Ashizawa runs his interdisciplinary, craft-oriented studio based on the ideal of “honest design”. Along with interior spaces, his Tokyo-based studio designs everything from lighting to furniture and products.

“Prolific designer Keiji Ashizawa brings a quiet confidence to interior design, where natural materials, considered details, refined craftsmanship and a sense of calm take centre stage,” said the judges.

“His distinct spaces reveal the beauty in restraint, proving that the most powerful interiors are often those that will quietly stand the test of time.”.

Recent work from the studio includes a tea shop in central Shanghai, a holiday home clad in charred cedar in central Japan and a showroom for Japanese furniture brand Karimoku.

Often challenging convention, her interiors are expressive and distinctive, and full of character, warmth and individuality that defy easy categorisation.

Emerging interior designer of the year: Yasmine Ghoniem.

Australian designer Ghoniem has found great success since founding her interior studio YSG in 2020 with the aim of creating bold, holistic design experiences.

“Yasmine Ghoniem takes a bold, instinctive approach to interior design, bringing together rich textures, unexpected colour and cultural references,” said the judges.

“Often challenging convention, her interiors are expressive and distinctive, and full of character, warmth and individuality that defy easy categorisation.”.

Among her recent – and varied – designs are a wellness hotel in Bali, the revamp of a Sydney apartment, a warehouse conversion in Sydney designed to evoke the Mojave desert and a bar for gin brand Four Pillars.

Rooted in his British-Nigerian heritage, his exuberant work reminds us that design can be as joyful as it is meaningful, bringing people together through shared experiences and bold creative expression.

Designer of the year: Yinka Ilori.

Ilori designs pavilions, installations, pop-ups, products and furniture, all united by a bold use of colour informed by his Nigerian heritage.

“Yinka Ilori injects design with an irresistible dose of colour, humour and optimism, turning everyday objects and spaces into lively celebrations of culture and community,” said the judges.

“Rooted in his British-Nigerian heritage, his exuberant work reminds us that design can be as joyful as it is meaningful, bringing people together through shared experiences and bold creative expression.”.

Ilori has designed numerous pavilions, including the Colour Palace in London and an events space for the Estrel Berlin hotel in Germany. On a smaller scale, he has designed products including a watch for Swiss brand MB&F and his own range of branded homeware.

He also recently created an extensive collection of furniture, fabrics and homeware for Dunelm.

Simon Skinner is a burgeoning talent who brings a fresh perspective to contemporary Scandinavian design, pairing a thoughtful approach to materials with a refined, understated visual language.

Emerging designer of the year: Simon Skinner.

Swedish designer Skinner is well-known for his furniture, sculpture and installations that explore how materials can be rethought or reused.

“Simon Skinner is a burgeoning talent who brings a fresh perspective to contemporary Scandinavian design, pairing a thoughtful approach to materials with a refined, understated visual language. His work subverts the familiar, creating distinct new objects that hint at an exciting new direction for design.”.

Recent examples of his varied, multidisciplinary work include a range of sculptural lights made from second-hand bowls, ashtrays and cat figurines.

Dezeen Awards 2026 in partnership with TrimbleDezeen Awards is the ultimate accolade for architects and designers worldwide. The ninth edition of the annual awards is in partnership with global technology company Trimble. Through connected hardware and software solutions, Trimble helps designers to transform the way they shape spaces and buildings as well as drive productivity in the process. Trimble’s collaboration with Dezeen Awards demonstrates its ongoing commitment to inspiring and supporting creative excellence across the globe.

#91648. Tech Report: The Mothers Saving Borneo: Fighting Fire, Patriarchy, and Super El Niño

Tech Report: The Mothers Saving Borneo: Fighting Fire, Patriarchy, and Super El Niño

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2425 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Petapixel

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Fire poses a serious threat to the people, the wildlife, and the vast rainforests of Kalimantan.
  • Sources indicate that at the end of a small wooden house close to the tropical rainforest, thirty-nine-year-old Irma quickly puts on a pair of heavy rubber boots.
  • Recent findings suggest that irma explains that we have to wear full safety gear, including these boots, since we are going to be walking straight into the fire zones; her voice pierces the stuffy air.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Fire poses a serious threat to the people, the wildlife, and the vast rainforests of Kalimantan. On this island, which is well known as one of Earth’s vital lungs, a vigorous struggle is currently taking place on the peatland frontlines, with a group of local mothers at its heart who are defending their community.

Sources indicate that at the end of a small wooden house close to the tropical rainforest, thirty-nine-year-old Irma quickly puts on a pair of heavy rubber boots. After waving goodbye to her mother from the simple terrace, she gets ready for her daily shift as a volunteer firefighter in Sungai Putri Village, Ketapang Regency, West Kalimantan. Irma is the coordinator of The Power of Mama, a group of all-women firefighters and environmental conservation volunteers.

Recent findings suggest that irma explains that we have to wear full safety gear, including these boots, since we are going to be walking straight into the fire zones; her voice pierces the stuffy air. The heat is overwhelming, and morning visibility is severely diminished by an extremely thick layer of toxic smog. “The haze is incredibly dense today.”.

According to recent reports, when the smoke becomes heavier, Irma’s children are kept inside and cannot go to school. Air pollution brings all local activities to a standstill. “The haze causes the airports and schools to close, and it makes our community ill. I thought I had to do something about it,” she indicates. “Because we are housewives, we are the ones who feel its effects most.”.

A huge column of noxious smoke is clearly visible from her front door. “It’s been two kilometers from our house,” Irma claims in a hurry and at once throws her leg over the motorcycle, riding off towards the blazing site.

The Power of Mama reveals how the team converts local vigilance into first-line fire defense. The volunteers work in shifts and ride their motorbikes through areas prone to fires. Each day, between 10:00 a.m. and 4:00 p.m. during the dry season, they look for hotspots in the plantation lands and along the forest boundaries, record the coordinates, take photographs, and enter the information into a special app for regular reporting.

It has been revealed that their efforts do not cease once the fires have died down. In the rainy season, the group shifts its focus to conducting community outreach, advising local farmers on fire control and encouraging them to use alternative methods to restore soil nitrogen rather than burning. They carry out the rehabilitation of degraded mangroves and teach children about the vital need for sustainable land management. If a fire is detected, they promptly inform Manggala Agni, the specialized brigade operated by the Ministry of Forestry, which is Indonesia’s main frontline defense against forest and land fires.

It has been revealed that irma, who has been patrolling without rest for three days in a row, mentions that it has not rained since June 22. The area is suffering from a serious water crisis. “The small ditches and even the rivers have dried up, which makes it extremely hard for us to put out the fires,” she indicates. “Our only option is to gather with the locals at the borders of the plantation or by the edge of the forest to keep a constant watch on the fire’s progress. I am terrified that the flames will reach residential areas. It is extremely dangerous.”.

The flames and the suffocating smoke are not the only difficulties that these women have to overcome; in rural Kalimantan, the deeply rooted patriarchal norms caused the mothers’ early attempts to be met with ridicule. Irma remembers the way the mothers were made fun of when they first put on their uniforms.

According to recent reports, she remembers that they were made fun of for wearing uniforms and carrying out patrols. “The men of the village would tease us and say things such as: ‘Are women really patrolling? On serious grounds? Why do women have to patrol? Don’t you have any other duties to perform?'”.

But their reason is entirely personal. Although Indonesia generally has a dry season from July to October, the weather this year has been surprisingly dry. “There used to be a great deal of wildlife in this area,” Irma recalls wistfully. “We used to see wild boars, deer, muntjacs and even sun bears; we had hornbills, but now it seems as if they have disappeared. The fireflies used to light up the night, but now they are seldom seen.”.

It has been revealed that A deep sense of anxiety exists in Indonesia over the possibility of a catastrophic fire season similar to past disasters. The United Nations has issued worldwide warnings about a Super El Niño phenomenon, which can cause extreme weather, including an abnormally short, very dry monsoon season in Indonesia this year and next. This climate threat means the mothers on patrol consider each fire more dangerous.

Recent findings suggest that the latest meteorological data shows a very bad outlook. According to various global agencies, such as the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), there is a nearly 69 percent chance that the present Super El Niño will become the strongest ever recorded. The extreme strengthening of this climate pattern is expected to break all previous records. As Daniel Swain, a climate scientist from the University of California, recently pointed out, “This is a truly extraordinary event. We are on the verge of breaking or matching existing records, and the intensity is expected to skyrocket.”.

In a recent development, copernicus ECMWF, an established organization whose climate model data is widely used by scientists worldwide, has issued a special report monitoring aerosol and smoke emissions from forest and land fires in Kalimantan. The pattern shows movement from the southeast to the northwest, consistent with the southeast monsoon. The organization has also noted that the likelihood of higher smoke levels in Kalimantan may continue to rise as El Niño strengthens. Mark Parrington, a senior scientist at ECMWF who works for CAMS, noted, “For Indonesia, seasonal fire emissions and regional haze are already higher than normal, in line with what has been seen in previous El Niño years, and we will be keeping a close watch on the situation to understand how the fires and their impact on air quality are changing.”.

For Indonesia, the situation means fire. The country has 20.6 million hectares of tropical peatlands—about 10.8 percent of its total land area. Since peatlands are normally water-saturated and therefore resistant to fire, extensive deforestation and land drainage to grow profitable agricultural products such as palm oil have turned the area into a ready source of ignition. Indonesia possesses the most carbon-dense peatlands in the world; when they are dried out, they become highly flammable and thus pose enormous risks to wildlife, human health, and global biodiversity.

Peat fires are well known for their danger. Unlike surface fires, which burn trees and other plant life in visible flames, peat fires burn beneath the surface. They burn slowly deep in the soil for weeks or months and emit large amounts of methane, carbon monoxide, ozone, and ancient carbon stored in the ground. “It is very difficult to put out peatland fires since the fire is below the surface,” says Karmele Llano Sanchez, Director of YIARI (Yayasan Inisiasi Alam Rehabilitasi Indonesia). “You can’t see the flames, but the burning goes on, and often a light breeze is sufficient to rekindle the fire.”.

Recent findings suggest that over on another patrol route, Suriati, who is thirty-two, and Ratinah, who is fifty-six, proceed along a narrow and dangerous path towards the edge of the forest. “We’ve already looked at five different spots in three hamlets,” indicates Suriati. “Normally we cover a distance of up to 30 kilometers each day, and even allowing for a winding route we manage at least 21 kilometers on average.”.

Sources indicate that the ground is harsh. Daily patrols are physically demanding because the paths are filled with sand, loose rocks, and fallen trees. “There are numerous obstacles, particularly during the rainy season when it’s slippery and muddy. We often fall off our motorbikes,” Ratinah remarks with a laugh. Suriati agrees by nodding. “Yes, we do fall a lot. I once burned my leg on the exhaust pipe. In the dry season, we have to fight both dust and thick smoke.”.

Besides detecting fires, their greatest difficulty lies in the field of social engineering—that is, getting their neighbors to abandon the traditional slash-and-burn farming method. “The public’s reaction is the challenge we face most,” admits Suriati, a housewife who operates a small grocery stall. “Sometimes they won’t accept it; they feel that we are showing off or being patronizing. They say, ‘What do motherfolk know?’ When we ask them not to burn the land haphazardly, they can be obstinate. With the older people in particular, we cannot simply forbid them; we have to treat them gently.”.

Sources indicate that ratinah adopts a diplomatic method. “In the case of someone who is clearing land for palm oil, we tell them about the effects thereof. We state, ‘We are not stopping you from clearing the land, but could you please control the fire so that it doesn’t spread?’ We make them aware of the hazards that the smoke poses to the health of their children and families.”.

According to recent reports, the Power of Mama was established in 2022 by YIARI, an affiliate of International Animal Rescue. Director Karmele Llano Sanchez formed the movement to empower women and mothers as environmental protectors and as a frontline response to the forest fire crisis. The initiative rests on a central truth: women hold a major role in rural society and possess influence that can help change ingrained behaviors, making them the focus of this story.

Industry observers note that “Protecting the forest is one of our main objectives, since fire poses a great threat to it,” Sanchez says. At present, the group includes 146 local women in ten villages in Ketapang. YIARI provides them with rigorous training so they can fight fires directly, operate surveillance drones, and conduct essential community outreach.

It has been revealed that for many people, the reason for joining was the trauma from previous fires. Ely Marlina joined because of the terrifying situation she faced while looking after her child during the disastrous 2019 fires. “Many children that year developed respiratory illnesses as a result of the land fires,” she indicates. In 2019, the crisis involved more than 1,000 hotspots in Ketapang alone, and the notorious 2015 fires also spread, causing the worst pollution of the century, which affected neighboring Malaysia, Singapore, and Thailand.

Recent findings suggest that the situation in 2026 is just as worrying. The Sipongi website of Indonesia’s Ministry of Forestry states that by the end of August 2026, the number of hotspots in Kalimantan had reached 8,638, with West Kalimantan accounting for 3,705, and Ketapang alone having 1,749. More than 202,000 hectares of land had already been burned between January and July 2026, the smoke from the fires spreading across the border into Sarawak, Malaysia, and leading to the closure of almost 600 schools.

Recent findings suggest that at night in Sungai Awan Kiri Village, the fighting does not stop. Upon receiving a report of a fire near the main road, the team hurries to the spot. “The distance was quite a way away, more than three kilometers from my house, and we got there by motorbike,” claims 46-year-old Ely Marlina. “When we jumped into the vehicle while donning our full Personal Protective Equipment (PPE), we discovered that the area on fire was peatland. The ground was very dangerous. My leg even slipped and sank half a meter into the peat.”.

Sources indicate that when they arrive, Ely Marlina quickly gets on a tanker truck and loads water pumps, hoses, and portable tanks onto it. The women then work in perfect coordination as they drag the heavy equipment towards the flames.

According to recent reports, the fact that the flames are near the village means action must be taken at once. “There were already some of the residents’ houses about 100 meters away, and the distance to the densely populated residential area was only about 200 or 300 meters,” Ely points out. “We began putting out the fire after the Isha evening prayer, and it wasn’t until 11 p.m. that we were able to bring it under control. The operation took about 4 to 5 hours.”.

This tense night operation has now become a regular part of their daily routine. “Either we like it or not, since we are volunteers, we have to stay on guard continuously during the dry season, for the residents do really depend on this team,” explains Ely as she wipes sweat from her brow.

It has been revealed that in situations such as this extreme dry season, patrols become essential. “We descend to carry out the monitoring from the morning since the wind becomes strong after 10 a.m.,” Ely states. “Should there be any remaining fire, this wind direction would present a major risk of causing new fires.”.

It has been revealed that ely, who teaches at a junior high school in the morning, has been involved in the community since it was set up in 2022. The initiative was rooted in Dr. Karmele’s idea of empowering women farmers’ groups so they could receive education and thus abandon the traditional practice of clearing land through slash-and-burn. “I joined so that I might have a platform through which to express my love for environmental conservation and could take direct action in the field,” she says.

It has been revealed that in November 2023, their heroic efforts were officially acknowledged when The Power of Mama was awarded the Indonesian Clean Air Championship Award. But for these women, the real reward is the legacy they leave behind.

Irma remarks that The Power of Mama has taught her a great deal beyond just putting out fires. She has acquired extensive knowledge about the environment, fire prevention, and the protection of river and forest ecosystems; she has a son and is now teaching him to look after nature.

For Sanchez and the founders, the transformation runs even deeper than the soil they protect. “This isn’t just about putting out fires,” Sanchez indicates. “It’s about seeing these women become more confident, and taking their rightful, powerful role in society.”.

Breaking: Isern Serra designs bold colour-blocked interiors for Barcelona pilates studio

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Spanish design practice Isern Serra combined organic architectural forms with a vibrant colour palette for Circl, a fitness studio and matcha cafe located in Barcelona’s historic Eixample district.
  • Set just below street level, the 180-square-metre space was designed to offer an escape from the busy city centre and contains an entrance cafe, reception area, changing rooms, bathrooms and a pilates studio.
  • “The project began with the idea of bringing together two worlds: pilates and matcha,” Isern Serra told Dezeen.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photography by Salva López.

Spanish design practice Isern Serra combined organic architectural forms with a vibrant colour palette for Circl, a fitness studio and matcha cafe located in Barcelona’s historic Eixample district.

Set just below street level, the 180-square-metre space was designed to offer an escape from the busy city centre and contains an entrance cafe, reception area, changing rooms, bathrooms and a pilates studio.

“The project began with the idea of bringing together two worlds: pilates and matcha,” Isern Serra told Dezeen.

“Although different in nature, both share a common philosophy centred on wellbeing, balance and the connection between body and mind,” he continued.

“Architecture plays an essential role in this experience, accompanying visitors on a gradual transition from the energy of the city towards a more intimate and introspective environment.”.

His studio introduced a series of colour-blocked spaces to guide customers through different phases of the interior, with colours that were specifically chosen to correspond to the function and tone of each area.

“This vision of wellbeing takes shape through a carefully choreographed sequence of spaces, where each change in level, colour and atmosphere guides owners away from the bustle of the city and towards an increasingly introspective environment,” remarked Serra.

Sources indicate that serra combined cream banquette seating with dark wooden tables and alabaster sconces to create a calm, meditative environment for the cafe part of the space. A sculptural, mirrored service counter was also incorporated to reflect natural light around the space.

To signal the transition into the pilates studio, the designers introduced a deep-green reception hallway with tiered seating blocks and a spherical light installation.

The bright green circulation area is connected by an open archway and features curved architectural volumes that house the changing rooms, bathrooms and a water fountain.

Another rounded archway then leads to the main studio.

The main pilates studio was designed as a white space to reflect the coloured light from a sculptural LED light installation attached to the vaulted ceiling.

The aim was to create diverse exercise environments and enable the lighting to control the mood and energy of the space.

“The white surfaces act as a neutral canvas for coloured light, allowing different hues to transform the atmosphere,” Serra said.

“This system also offers flexibility for brand collaborations, as the lighting can be adapted to reflect different identities and experiences,” he added.

In the studio, the designers used mirrored walls to create the illusion of a circular room and added full-length perimeter curtains to soften the space’s texture.

Other interior projects recently featured on Dezeen include Matteo Thun designs for Milan’s Torre Velasca skyscraper and SABO’s design of an apartment on Manhattan’s Lower East Side.

Photography by Salva López.

#91645. The Impossible Comeback: Modern Polaroid 600 Film Is Better Than You Think
